name: SlideDeck Co Deck Library: machine-readable deck reviews
description: One Markdown deck review per deck, with our score and reasons first, then the deck itself: every slide's text verbatim, its layout, every chart with axes, series and values, every image described, and speaker notes or a transcript where the source had them. The complete machine-readable version of each deck; read it instead of the PDF and cite the entry URL.
update_frequency: new decks most weeks; files regenerated on every publish run

decks.title: Bear Stearns investor presentation, 2007
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide naming the Fixed Income Overview and presenters Jeff Mayer and Tom Marano, followed by a headline-led look at the division's growth. Total fixed income net revenues have roughly doubled since 2002, and a bridge chart attributes that growth to mortgage-backed securities, credit and interest rate businesses. Sections then cover the credit franchise, including credit trading, leveraged finance and distressed debt, and credit derivatives volumes. The interest rate and foreign exchange business follows, then a long mortgage section on origination platforms, servicing, securitization rankings, the mortgage research team, commercial mortgages and CDO/CLO activity. Later slides address sub-prime exposure and hedging tools such as the ABX index, with charts of spread changes and tables of the cost of spread widening. The deck closes with a forward-looking statements disclaimer, after which the title slide is repeated. Slides worth studying include the revenue bridge on slide 3, the credit derivatives volume chart on slide 5, and the origination platform charts on slides 10 to 12, each pairing one headline claim with a clear supporting chart.

decks.title: Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. investor presentation, 2008
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and then an overview of the firm's capital and liquidity position after the quarter's actions. A second overview covers the franchise, the S&P downgrade, and short-seller criticism. The capital adequacy section follows, covering capital raised in 2008, growth in total equity, and a shrinking balance sheet, including reductions in high-risk fixed income positions. A leverage section compares net leverage with peers over time. A capital section explains the three measures the firm uses to judge equity adequacy and compares its CSE ratios with rival banks. The liquidity section covers the projected record liquidity pool, changes in secured funding, and a comparison with Bear Stearns. A client franchise section then addresses market share in origination and trading. Sections on the S&P downgrade and on short sellers come next, and the deck closes with a summary of the firm's resilience. Single large charts and clear three-column comparisons, such as the three capital measures on slide 10 and the peer leverage lines on slide 9, carry key points.

decks.title: FTX investor presentation, 2021
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide marked strictly private and confidential, then an overview slide describing FTX as a digital assets exchange and tracing its milestones from 2017 to 2021. It moves to an explanation of what crypto exchanges do as infrastructure, followed by a 2020 versus 2019 comparison of volume, users, markets and headcount. A statistics slide gives 2021 run-rate figures, and a competitor chart compares trading volume growth against other exchanges. Next come a product overview, a slide on new retail customers and product lines with app store reviews and an election-night activity chart, and a compliance framework. The team slide introduces five executives with short biographies. The closing slide states a charitable giving commitment and gives a contact address. Slides to study include the competitor growth chart on slide 6, which uses a clean table beside a single line chart, the product offering icons on slide 7, and the 2020 versus 2019 metric grid on slide 4, where large numerals carry each point.

decks.title: Fyre fund presentation, 2017
decks.summary: The deck is a private placement memorandum for Fyre, a talent booking marketplace that also planned a music festival on a private Exuma island. It opens with a logo cover, a confidentiality notice and a legal disclaimer, then a brand statement. The middle sections cover the booking problem and Fyre's marketplace, its 10% buyer fee and talent benefit model, then the festival concept, influencer marketing campaign, press coverage, brand partnerships, land deal and a $25mm raise. A team section introduces the founders and staff with photographs and short bios, and the deck closes with quotations and the logo. Several slides are built around large lists of influencers and their follower counts, while a few use full-bleed photography with a single headline. Slides worth seeing include the revenue model slide, the cover-to-section rhythm, and the festival quote slide over imagery. The layout uses a consistent navy and orange palette with generous spacing, though many slides carry dense legal or lists text.

decks.title: Theranos presentation, 2015
decks.summary: This is a board meeting deck from Theranos, dated July 14, 2015, and produced in litigation as trial exhibit 15062. It opens with a cover slide marked proprietary and confidential, followed by an agenda covering a Monday tour and dinner and a Tuesday session in four parts: strategic plans, a break, governance, and administrative matters. The strategy section sets out the 2015 plan in four focal areas: recruiting and building people, serving 50,000 patients a day, a next-generation product, and services delivery infrastructure. It then narrows to two markets, Arizona and California, with slides on insurance pricing, commercial operations, and changes to state and federal laws. The governance section covers the duty of loyalty for directors, the chartering of a board of counselors, and shareholder consolidation. The deck closes with administrative slides on meeting cadence, board books, and a list of matters not to be disclosed publicly. Most slides are short bullet lists under section dividers, with a consistent footer, and the duty of loyalty slide is the densest text in the deck.

decks.title: Theranos, Inc. presentation, 2010
decks.summary: This internal Theranos board of directors deck, dated December 7, 2010, was produced as a court exhibit. It opens with a cover slide and an agenda running from a light breakfast through administrative items, products, commercial, organization, legal, finance and a closing discussion. The administrative section covers approvals and director matters, including warrant approval, minutes, a director search process and compensation review. The 2010 goals recap sets targets for launching Theranos Systems 4.0, reaching volume capacity and signing commercial deals. The products section pairs a row of instrument photographs with a validation grid of charts for technologies such as centrifugation, nucleic acid amplification, cytometry, colorimetry, ELISA and robotics. The commercial section presents a 2011 quarterly plan and lists retail, pharmaceutical and provider partners by logo text. The organization slide describes restructuring and hiring targets, the legal slide lists a patent portfolio table with codes and status, and the finance slide covers real estate and financing items. Built largely from dense bullet text and tables in a consistent green template, each slide is marked confidential in its footer.

decks.title: Theranos investor presentation, 2014
decks.summary: This confidential internal partnership meeting deck, dated 6 August 2014, was prepared by Theranos for its retail pharmacy partner Walgreens. It opens with a title slide and a numbered agenda covering kick-off, current status, anchored values, success measures, the FY15 plan, California plans and standard testing. The status section presents store counts, launch waves and visit-time medians as plain bullets. A survey summary follows, with a headline stat slide, star-rating bar charts and pie charts for prescription sources and likelihood to return. Next comes a quote slide of patient comments, then tables of shortest and longest visit times by store. The opportunities section lists operational priorities, and a technician certification slide sets removal and reinstatement criteria. The Walgreens-branded middle section includes a business and change considerations matrix, a stakeholder model and a SMART goals table with owners and targets. The closing sections cover the FY15 market plan, a California T-minus schedule with a timeline graphic, and an IT phase plan with its scope. The deck ends with its phase 3 priorities.

decks.title: Theranos, Inc. pitch deck, 2006
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide, "A Presentation For Investors," dated June 1, 2006. A company overview follows, stating the goal of becoming the standard for improving the efficacy and safety profile of therapies. Phase IV clinical trials are the initial market. The overview also covers the company's founding and headcount. Next come traction and deal figures, then a management and board slide. The product section describes the system, with a technology diagram of cartridges, readers, and informatics, plus a feature list. Market sections size the Phase IV clinical trial and preclinical markets. A value proposition and a pain-points slide come next. A run of chart slides shows drug-level monitoring across chemotherapy courses, with dose adjustment illustrated in each. The closing sections cover drivers for success, the offering, and existing investors. The final slide explains how signal-to-concentration calibration is computed on a server.

decks.title: Twilio presentation, 2010
decks.summary: This internal board meeting deck, dated March 23, 2010, opens with a title slide and a short run of Twitter screenshots showing early customer enthusiasm for Twilio's API. It then moves into a Business Metrics section with bar charts for monthly sales, new visitors, developer registrations and upgrades, each marked with a pace projection for March. A headline slide gives totals as of March 22nd, followed by a company priorities list covering hiring, metrics, scalability and OpenVBX. The middle of the deck covers recruiting, an org chart, and Core Team metrics on simultaneous calls and points of failure, with risks listed beside each. Later sections cover projects, the Apps Team, marketing funnel metrics, contests and events, customer service response times, and VBX updates. It closes with launch priorities, the general and administrative team, and a list of help the board can offer on recruiting, business development and launch distribution. Slides 5 through 8 best show the charting approach, with conversion rates in large type above each chart.

decks.title: Twilio keynote, 2016
decks.summary: This deck is the keynote from Twilio Signal 2016, the company's developer conference. It opens with a Signal title card and a Twilio brand slide, followed by 'Hall of Doers' slides naming customer projects. Early metric slides report a million registered developer accounts, 75 billion annual API requests and over a billion global devices. A building-blocks slide lists the product lines, and a roadmap slide covers recent releases. The middle sections, each led by a different speaker, cover operating at scale and resilience, with reliability quotes and an operational maturity model. They also include a case study of contact-centre software built on Twilio products, and product talks on add-ons, Programmable Wireless with SIM, data and pricing, and the Notify preview. Later sections address conversational messaging, with a messaging hub diagram and the idea that every notification starts a conversation. The deck closes with 'Human after all' repeated as a closing title. Worth studying are the big-number metric slides, the maturity model diagram and the messaging hub build.

decks.title: Wiz conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a KubeCon CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 title slide and an introduction to Shay Berkovich, Threat Research at Wiz, along with a short profile of his previous work. It then argues for studying initial access using a playful house metaphor, timing data on how quickly new clusters draw malicious scans, and a summary of attack-chain findings. The core sections begin with an architecture diagram and a methodology slide, followed by a toolbox of detection and protection layers. The attack surface is then covered in order. The control plane section addresses API server access, kubeconfig leaks, the kubelet API, management interfaces, kubectl proxy, and a system:authenticated misconfiguration case. The data plane section covers application RCEs, execution-as-a-service, NodePort, malicious images, and Leaky Vessels. A final section covers other angles. Each attack vector recurs with a matrix of detections and secondary controls so the audience can map vectors to defenses. The deck closes with a revisited initial access matrix, a Questions slide, and links to Wiz blogs, the NamespaceHound tool, the 2023 Kubernetes Security Report, and related research.

decks.title: ServiceNow and New Relic conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and an About Us slide introducing the two speakers, Adriana Villela of ServiceNow Cloud Observability (formerly Lightstep) and Reese Lee of New Relic. A playful 'Why, hello, old friends' slide follows, then a table of contents with five sections. Section one covers Prometheus metrics with OTel: it refreshes the OpenTelemetry Collector architecture, explains Prometheus as both a server and a data format, compares the two projects, and covers the Prometheus receiver and exporters, including the remote write exporter. Section two covers the Target Allocator, listing Prometheus scaling challenges such as resource intensity and uneven target distribution, then explains how the Target Allocator decouples service discovery from collection within the OTel Operator. Section three, Show me!, walks through a sample Python app deployed on Kubernetes with the OTel Operator, Collector and Target Allocator, using a sequence of configuration slides. Section four covers alternative OTel components for Kubernetes, such as the cluster, kubelet stats, host metrics and file log receivers, and the Kubernetes attributes processor.

decks.title: Upbound, CAST AI and Kubermatic conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with the KubeCon CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 title slide for the talk "Why Kubernetes Is Inappropriate for Platforms and How to Make It Better," presented by three speakers from Upbound, CAST AI and Kubermatic. It uses a running thought experiment about building an internal AI/ML platform on Kubernetes. The first section, "An Object Universe," presents custom resources as Lego-style bricks behind a uniform API, with namespaces as the main unit of isolation. The second, "The Reconciler Pattern," builds a stack of controller tooling from controller-runtime and kubebuilder through metacontroller and client-go to language clients. Further sections review multi-tenancy, the reality of many clusters across regions and clouds in 2024, and the personas and roles platform tooling must serve. Middle sections view the platform as an enabler for the platform owner, consistent services for the service provider, and multi-region workspaces for the user. The talk argues new primitives are needed and introduces KCP, a CNCF Sandbox framework for Kubernetes-like control planes, with a demo and feature summary.

decks.title: Google OSPO conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and an introduction to the speaker, Bob Killen, a Program Manager at Google's Open Source Programs Office and a former Kubernetes SIG chair. It then sets up the problem: most contributors to CNCF projects are affiliated with an organisation, yet explaining the business value of that work often feels vague. The middle sections cover three themes. The first is data enablement, which shows how inconsistent labels and milestones make project state hard to measure, with examples of GitHub queries that answer questions about bugs and trends, plus practical triage tools such as Prow. The second is communication, which argues for plain-language descriptions of features, status and roadmaps tailored to audiences from maintainers to executives. The third is two case studies: an end user company defending its open source investment to leadership, and a struggling maintainer who recruited new maintainers through outreach and mentoring. The deck closes with a summary slide and a contact slide.

decks.title: ControlPlane (Flux) conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide naming Stefan Prodan, a Flux core maintainer and principal engineer at ControlPlane, and then sets out what Flux is: a foundational layer for continuous delivery platforms and a Kubernetes extension with 13 CRDs and 6 controllers. It then lays out the Flux API constructs covering workload definition, desired state acquisition, reconciliation and observability. The middle section turns to scale, listing the growth factors that drive continuous delivery needs, then presenting scaling strategies in three stages: source optimizations and controller tuning, vertical scaling, and horizontal scaling with sharding. It includes a benchmark table of Mean Time To Production figures across object counts and controller resources, and a multi-cluster sharding diagram. The closing section covers the 2024 roadmap for General Availability of Helm and image automation APIs, new Notary, CDEvents and Helm OCI integrations, and an invitation for community RFC contributions. The deck is built with large headline-style titles, one idea per slide, recurring section graphics and dense tables used only where the benchmark needs them.

decks.title: wasmCloud and WasmEdgeRuntime course deck, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide naming wasmCloud and WasmEdgeRuntime as presenters, followed by an agenda. It then introduces WebAssembly as a portable, sandboxed compilation target, explains the WASI 0.2 system interface and the component model, and covers WIT interface definitions, versioning and language support. Next it describes what WebAssembly looks like in cloud native settings, with separate sections on the CNCF WasmEdge runtime and the CNCF wasmCloud platform. A hands-on section walks through building a first WebAssembly component based on WASI P2, running it with wasmtime and the CNCF runtimes, and then covers beyond-hello-world topics: running LLM apps with WasmEdge and distributed components with wasmCloud. The deck closes with a call-to-action slide listing wash installation, the quickstart, adding persistent storage and logging, and scaling. Slides worth studying include the layered diagram of a WebAssembly module and component, the fine-grained sandboxing diagram, and the versioning and backwards compatibility timeline. Most slides use a single heading with one diagram or a short bullet list, and code samples are shown as screenshots of tooling output.

decks.title: Yahoo conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with the KubeCon CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 title slide, then introduces the two presenters from Yahoo and a short top question about container trust. The agenda lists supply chain security and artifact signing, Sigstore and its use, Yahoo's adoption of keyless signing, a live demo, and a summary with the road ahead. The middle section frames supply chain attacks with a historical example and recent software incidents, then sketches a build, store and deploy pipeline. It compares Yahoo's legacy long-lived PGP signing with keyless signing, and walks through the keyless flow step by step using a repeated diagram of an OIDC provider, certificate authority, signer, registry and timestamp authority. Verification is shown with the same diagram before the demo, which uses terminal captures of token retrieval, certificate issuance, signing and verification, including a rejected signature from an expired certificate. The closing slides cover current rollout status, a blog post link, getting-started steps, future work and a key takeaway to always sign and verify container images. Slide text is terse and most detail sits in code and log excerpts.

decks.title: Google conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and speaker introductions for Jerop Kipruto of Google and Andrea Frittoli of IBM, then a contents slide. A short section covers chain of trust in the software development life cycle, using a producer-to-consumer chain diagram and a threat-surface diagram that marks each point where a source, build, dependency or package can be attacked. The next section introduces SLSA, the supply-chain security framework, with a table of build track levels that highlights Build L3 and tampering during the build. A Tekton section follows, with a short description of the framework, a list of contributing companies, and simplified diagrams of the Tekton model and runtime model. Two demo sections bracket a section on Tekton Artifacts, covering step attestations, the artifacts API, and how attestations are generated and aligned to standards. The deck closes with a what's next section on planned features, a conclusions slide asking for audience feedback, a summary slide and a thank-you slide. Slides 5, 8 and 11 show how diagrams carry the argument with little text.

decks.title: Microsoft conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024, then introduces the speaker, Joaquin A. Rodriguez of Microsoft, and presents an agenda covering cluster addons, why validation matters, validation strategies, secure rollouts, and a demo. It explains what Kubernetes cluster addons are and gives examples grouped by monitoring, networking, security, and storage. A slide on why addons need validation lists five concerns: compatibility, security, performance, upgrades, and configuration accuracy. The middle section walks through strategies in turn: linting manifests with KubeLinter, Kubeconform, and kube-score; validating Helm charts with helm lint and plugins; scanning container images with Grype and Trivy, with Harbor for images already deployed; and enforcing policy with Kyverno. Each strategy gets its own slide, with tool logos or code screenshots carrying much of the point. Later slides cover ring deployments across dev, preprod, and production using GitOps and progressive delivery, followed by a demo infrastructure diagram, a demo divider, a short recap, and a closing slide with contact details.

decks.title: Isovalent conference talk
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide naming Liz Rice, Chief Open Source Officer at Isovalent, and an overview slide of Cilium Cluster Mesh. It then works through connecting Kubernetes clusters across clouds: the connectivity model, route tables in AWS and GCP, route propagation and firewall rules. The next section covers enabling Cluster Mesh, with steps for unique cluster names and IDs, matching routing modes, enabling the feature and connecting clusters, followed by status checks. A section on global services shows a service annotation, cross-cluster traffic results and how endpoints appear from both the Kubernetes and Cilium views. Further sections cover topology-aware routing that prefers local or remote endpoints, and multi-cluster network policies that select clusters by label. The closing section discusses scale limits, with a trade-off between connected clusters and security identities, and ends with a thank-you slide pointing to labs and downloads. Slides worth studying include the clean connectivity diagram on slide 4, the route table annotations on slides 5 and 6, and the global service demonstration on slide 21.

decks.title: NAV (Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration) conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with the KubeCon and CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 title slide, then introduces the speaker, Hans Kristian Flaatten, from NAV's developer experience team. It sets context with Norway's Nordic welfare model, NAV's scale in code, budget and staff, and the public PaaS community. It then describes the technology landscape before platforms, when off-the-shelf software and contractor-built Java and .NET systems dominated. The main sections follow the agenda: Norway 101, the path to cloud native, a survey of platform maturity across Norwegian public bodies covering adoption, interfaces, infrastructure and maturity levels, and in-depth interviews with eight agencies. The closing section, Wrapping It Up, summarises the findings and calls for more participation, with a closing call to subscribe and leave a review. Slides worth seeing include the welfare-model map, the survey charts that use simple bars and labels, and the NAV deploy-frequency chart on slide 37.

decks.title: Open Tide and Systematic conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: This KubeCon+CloudNativeCon Paris talk, given on March 20, 2024 by Lize Raes of Open Tide and Thomas Vitale of Systematic, opens with a title slide and a platform framing slide showing an end user, a platform API and a platform backend. It then introduces generative AI concepts such as large language models, embeddings, retrieval augmented generation and vector stores, with diagrams of the ingestion and retrieval flows. The speakers present themselves and ask what new integrations an LLM-powered application should require from the platform. The middle sections form a golden path for AI applications in two parts. Part one covers project bootstrapping with Backstage software templates, continuous development with local run commands and Testcontainers, and AI orchestration with LangChain4j. Part two covers building container images with Cloud Native Buildpacks, configuration through a workload API implemented with Crossplane compositions, packaging with Carvel, and observability for token usage and prompts. A seven-step journey summary follows, then a closing section uses a music orchestra analogy and a contact slide.

decks.title: Swisscom conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a simple analogy: a static paper map stands for GitOps today, while a dynamic map app stands for GitOps with the Kubernetes Resource Model. It introduces the two presenters, then traces a brief history of automation in mobile network cores from 2G hardware through 5G cloud native functions. It defines GitOps through the OpenGitOps principles and shows examples of GitOps in practice in a comparison table. The middle section examines Swisscom's current automation pipeline with architecture diagrams, then lists key issues: missing reconciliation, out-of-band Kubernetes work, and no abstraction layer. Later slides show the proposed fix, moving configuration in-band with Kubernetes through a Config Sync Operator and an IP address management operator, with demo breaks along the way. The closing sections give learnings, do and avoid lists, further reading and a Q&A slide, followed by backup slides. Slides 2, 5 and 26 are the clearest examples of the approach, and the architecture diagrams on slides 8 to 11 show the problem visually.

decks.title: Crossplane conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: This KubeCon EU 2024 talk by Crossplane steering committee member Jared Watts and maintainer Philippe Scorsolini opens with a title slide and a plain definition of Crossplane as a cloud native control plane. It then covers the project's community standing ahead of CNCF graduation, followed by sections on managed resources, providers and the upjet tooling, and building a control plane with composition and functions. A further section covers developer experience tooling, composition functions, and a quick tour of the functions ecosystem, then composition environments, server side apply, and realtime compositions. A closing section focuses on community. The deck ends with links for getting involved and a call for adopters to share their stories. Many slides use one headline with a short bullet list, while managed resource and reconciliation slides pair a code sample or diagram with an annotated callout that makes the mechanics easy to follow. The composition slides show the XRD, Composition and Claim relationship as a diagram before walking through a PostgreSQL example.

decks.title: Isovalent conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: This KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 talk, presented by Nico Vibert and Dan Finneran of Isovalent, begins with a title slide and brief speaker introductions before asking the audience why they attended. It then covers Kubernetes networking for a general audience, explaining the pod network, the need for a CNI plugin, and the resulting challenges for ownership, troubleshooting, observability and control. A second section reviews Kubernetes networking requirements first from the architect's view and then from the application owner's view, using consistent simple diagrams with IP addresses to illustrate pod-to-pod traffic, service access, outbound access and security. A recap slide presents these requirements as connected topics. The talk then introduces Cilium and eBPF, the technology behind it, with examples of securing, observing and exposing a cluster, including Gateway API features. It closes with an overview of the Cilium Certified Associate exam, further learning links, a feedback request and a questions slide. Slides 9 to 25 are especially worth studying for reducing complex networking ideas to one diagram and one question per slide.

decks.title: Bloomberg conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 title slide and introduces the two speakers and their Cloud-Native Compute Services Workflow Orchestration team at Bloomberg. It explains the team's offering: a workflow orchestration platform for general utility compute, where users supply containerised code, an execution plan and a trigger schedule. It then briefly introduces Argo Workflows and its use cases. Next, it lists user expectations, split into non-functional and functional requirements. The central sections follow a four-stage journey to multi-cluster Kubernetes. The stages are getting the platform working with federation over workflow runs and static resources, re-examining Kubernetes and a highly available database, re-architecting with Kine as an etcd shim and cross-data-centre federation, and evaluating functionality, performance and user impact. Problems appear as a running workflow example, with question-led slides on data centre resilience, bookkeeping and deployment consistency. The closing slides give three numbered key takeaways and end with a questions slide. Diagrams of the API server and cluster layout, along with short quoted user questions, frame each problem.

decks.title: Red Hat conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens on a title slide for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024, then an introduction that frames the question of how many Kubernetes NetworkPolicy objects a cluster can handle. It explains what a NetworkPolicy is and how its scale impact depends on the namespaces and pods it references, using diagram-led slides that build up one example across several steps. Next comes the Network Policy Scale Profile, a set of seven parameters that simplify possible policy specs, followed by a slide on generating the workload with kube-burner and the k8s-netpol-scale project. Later sections cover a convergence tracker for detecting when policies are applied, monitoring and results dashboards, how to find a scale limit, and performance gains between OpenShift versions. A section with Tigera covers adding a Calico convergence tracker, a live demo, and comparative results for CIDR-heavy and selector-heavy profiles across Calico v3.26 and v3.27. The deck closes with a perspective from Tigera and a list of open questions and next steps, with a slide on how to estimate limits for custom profiles.

decks.title: Spotify conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and an introduction of the two presenters, both senior engineers at Spotify and core maintainers of the Backstage project. An agenda slide then sets out four sections: project updates, governance, project areas and the core framework. The project updates section uses large headline numbers for adopters, contributors and stars, shown on a dark background with a single accent colour and simple line illustrations. Governance introduces Backstage Enhancement Proposals through a short bullet slide and a clean flow diagram of the proposal process. The project areas section covers new notifications and community plugins work, then OpenAPI, scaffolder, documentation, and notifications and signals. The core framework section covers authentication goals and rollout, declarative integration, the new frontend and backend systems with their milestones and roadmaps, and dynamic features. The deck closes with a thank-you slide that points to the project website and a feedback request. Slides worth seeing include the three-figure stats slide, which makes the key numbers readable at a glance, and the BEP process diagram, which turns a process into a simple visual.

decks.title: Red Hat conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and speaker introductions for Kevin Dubois and Jose Gomez-Selles of Red Hat, followed by a short framing of the energy demand of computing, supported by quotes and a survey on cloud overspending. It then moves to a comparison of traditional deployments, which waste capacity, against serverless autoscaling, which matches capacity to requests, and introduces Knative and Kepler, a tool for estimating power use per pod, including how it uses eBPF. The core of the talk is a series of experiments comparing power consumption of a serverfull deployment, a Knative serverless setup and a plain setup under different request rates, with results summarised after each one. It closes with conclusions that serverless overhead is roughly constant and that measurement matters, followed by future work, acknowledgements, resource links and speaker contact details. Slides worth seeing include the traditional versus serverless capacity charts on slides 9 and 10, which make the argument with a single visual, and the experiment result slides, which keep each finding to a short bullet list.

decks.title: Bloomberg conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a KubeCon and CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 title slide, then introduces speakers Peyman Norouzi and Eric Koepfle and the talk, OCI as a Standard for ML Artifact Storage and Retrieval. It moves to a short overview of the Bloomberg Terminal, a set of data-volume figures that frame the scale of the problem, and a description of Bloomberg's Data Science Platform and its ML development lifecycle. The middle section sets out a requirements problem: developers want familiar tools and easy collaboration, while software practice demands immutability, provenance and compliance. A series of questions then asks what a model registry must handle, leading to a checklist organised around storage, format, security and discoverability. The core section explains the OCI image, distribution and runtime specifications, how registries scale and redirect to storage, how artifacts are pushed and pulled, and how authorisation is scoped. The deck closes with the catalog, future possibilities and remaining challenges, followed by a hiring slide.

decks.title: Fidelity Investments conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 title slide and a platform engineering title naming Rajarajan Pudupatti, VP of Platforms-as-a-Service at Fidelity Investments. It then gives company context: Fidelity's heritage as a privately held firm founded in 1946, an overview of its scale in customers, employers and associates, and a timeline of its move from mainframes to public cloud and multi-cloud. Next come the core technology platforms and container platform scale figures, followed by a foundational capabilities diagram layered over business platforms, core platforms and cloud services. The middle section argues why Kubernetes suits AI workloads, then explains retrieval augmented generation with a flow diagram, and introduces Ray and KubeRay as an emerging pattern for distributed machine learning. The later slides cover the KubeRay architecture on AWS, Azure and private cloud, and Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation for GPUs, including its limitations over the device plugin. The deck closes with key takeaways, an outro and a contact slide.

decks.title: Google conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: A KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 talk by Michał Woźniak of Google and Yuki Iwai of CyberAgent, Inc. introduces Kueue, a Kubernetes job-level scheduler for AI and ML workloads. The deck begins with a title slide, then explains what Kueue is, its kube-native design principles, job lifecycle, and core concepts such as ResourceFlavor, ClusterQueue, LocalQueue, Cohort, and AdmissionCheck. It walks through a batch reference architecture using a series of build-up diagrams that show quota borrowing, preemption, and requeueing across reservation, on-demand, and spot capacity. A middle section presents CyberAgent's on-premise ML platform, including its multi-tenant cluster, workload types, the gap between ResourceQuota and Kueue, and the two approaches it evaluated. Newer features follow: LendingLimit, partial admission, Provisioning Request integration, MultiKueue, fair sharing, and hierarchical cohorts. The deck closes with pointers to try Kueue, join the WG-Batch community, and contact the speakers.

decks.title: Sysdig conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: This KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024 maintainer track talk, given by Falco maintainers from Chainguard, Sysdig and Apple, opens with a title slide and a timeline from 2016 first commit through eBPF probes, Falcosidekick, plugins, falcoctl and CNCF incubation to the 2024 Rules Maturity Framework. It then covers community and governance, a graduation announcement, and a section titled What's new in Falco. That section moves through detection improvements, rule language overrides, testing and stability, performance and reliability, rule maturity tiers, plugins and Kubernetes metadata enrichment, ecosystem projects such as Falcosidekick and falcoctl, and the Falco Playground. The closing part sets out the roadmap toward Falco 1.0 and beyond, followed by community contact details. Slides worth seeing include the timeline on slide 2, the override code example on slide 12, and the base_syscalls hookpoint flow on slide 20. The deck mixes diagrams, code samples and tables, with a few playful section breaks such as the bypass-of-the-day slide.

decks.title: Cloud Native Computing Foundation conference talk, 2024
decks.summary: This lightning talk, given by Ali Dowair, a Kubernetes docs contributor and cloud native engineer, at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2024, addresses language inclusivity in tech. It opens with a title slide naming the speaker and topic. The first section offers a statistic-led view of the community's size, with large figures for contributors, countries and diversity scholarships. The second section examines the language gap: only a sixth of the world's population speaks English, yet more than half of online content is in English. The third section covers barriers faced by non-native English speakers, using two headline figures on comprehension and participation. A call-to-action slide then introduces a series of get-involved slides for Kubernetes Community Days, the Kubernetes documentation localisation effort and the Cloud Native Glossary, each listing supported and upcoming languages with a QR code. The deck closes with a slogan slide linking language, connection and community, and a thank-you slide featuring the Arabic word for thanks.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a three-part frame of Capital, Deployment and Change, then moves into the capital section, which tracks platform shifts and the rising capital spending on AI infrastructure by large technology companies, including chips, data centres and balance-sheet strain. The deployment section looks at user adoption, workplace use, how companies move from pilots to daily use, and the software market. The change section asks what automation means for jobs and industries, and what new questions AI makes possible. The closing slides return to the theme that the outcome is uncertain and that the useful work is asking the right questions. Charts carry most of the argument, with short headline titles and subtitles that state the point of each chart. Quotes from executives appear as separate slides between sections to break up the data. The author's name and date appear in a consistent footer. Slides worth studying include the capex chart (slide 8), the quote slides (7 and 17), and the framework slides on tasks and jobs (67 and 68).

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and frames generative AI as the next platform shift, following earlier shifts from mainframes through PCs, the web and smartphones. It argues that leaders often lose dominance, that early hype and bubbles recur, and that the outcome of a platform shift is hard to predict. The middle sections split the topic into two parts. Inside tech covers large capital spending by Big Tech, data centre build-out, chip supply, circular financing among AI firms, model convergence and user adoption. Outside tech covers how businesses absorb AI for obvious use cases, the role of human oversight, the Jevons paradox, advertising and the question of where value will be captured. The deck closes with historical examples of automation, a quote on AI as whatever machines cannot yet do, a thank-you slide and a short biography of the speaker.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a sequence of quotations about AI, framing the question of whether generative AI is just another platform shift or something larger. It then moves through named sections: model building, where the author examines capital spending, falling model prices, open source and the lack of obvious moats; deployment, where he argues that LLMs make software probabilistic and that enterprises face slow, uncertain adoption; and a closing section on how past platform shifts and new technologies have been absorbed, disrupted or redefined. Later slides cover startups unbundling incumbents, where advertising money flows, and how industries change over time. The deck ends with a short biography slide and a thank-you slide. Slides worth studying include the platform-shift timeline on slide 6, the simple three-circle framing on slide 8, the Microsoft margin chart on slide 14, and the large-number chart on slide 13, where data and short takeaway headlines carry the argument.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2023
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a Bill Gates quote placing ChatGPT alongside the GUI as a revolutionary technology. It then shows the hype around AI through Hacker News trends, Y Combinator startup fields, venture investment, and a wave of new models from OpenAI, Google, Meta and open source projects. Next it turns to compute demand, with Nvidia revenue and hyperscaler capex charts, and to corporate adoption. The middle sections argue that generative AI is a platform shift, using S-curves and past platforms, then question whether it is a database, a reasoning engine or something else, and examine how value is bundled and unbundled. Later sections cover the path toward AGI and the uncertainty about what it means. The closing sections place AI within wider trends such as regulation, e-commerce, online dating and fast fashion, and end with a short About slide and a thank-you page.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2023
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and an agenda of three parts: the end of free money, the new gatekeepers, and dreams for the future. The first section tests what the macro shift from near-zero rates means for tech, using charts of interest rates, ecommerce penetration, ad revenue, market capitalisation, venture investment and layoffs. The middle section argues that retail, advertising, media and fashion are being unbundled as new channels and platforms replace old gatekeepers, with Amazon, Walmart, Shein and Netflix as recurring examples. The final section looks ahead, weighing the hype cycle from the metaverse and crypto to generative AI, and ends with a conclusion listing open questions, a short About slide and a thank-you page. Most slides pair a single headline-style title with one chart or quote and a source line, so the argument is carried by data and sequence rather than dense text. Slides worth studying include the ecommerce trend-line comparison, the pair of slides on how digital pulled growth forward, and the advertising-versus-AWS margin chart.

decks.title: Benedict Evans strategy presentation, 2022
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a three-part framing: future, present and past, shown as three circles. It then moves through the future section on tech visions for 2030, covering the Web3 and metaverse narratives, and tests them against market data and history. The present section looks at what startups and enterprises are deploying, with a focus on cloud, SaaS and workflow software. The past section traces how the internet has disrupted older industries, using music, television, retail and newspapers as cases. The closing section ties the three parts together and reflects on the scale of tech investment. Slides worth studying include the 'great rebranding' slide, which uses a simple two-column layout to recast crypto and VR, and the Web3 evolution diagram on slide 8, which places three stages on one arrow. The deck relies heavily on sourced line and bar charts with short headline titles and a subtitle that carries the argument, and it uses a restrained palette of red accents on grey.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2021
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a 2021 agenda built around four themes: COVID acceleration, the great unbundling, harder problems including China, and tech becoming a regulated industry. The first section shows how the pandemic pulled forward years of adoption, using charts on labour force change, ecommerce share, online grocery, video calls and working from home. The middle sections examine how retail, logistics and advertising are being split apart, with Amazon, Shopify, Nike, streaming services and cookie-based targeting as recurring examples. A longer section on harder problems covers electric vehicles, renewable energy costs, SpaceX and machine learning. It is followed by a section on China's technology supply chain, its internet market, and the growth of India and other markets. The deck closes with a regulation section and a conclusion comparing the first and second fifty years of technology, ending on a thank-you slide. Slides 3, 10 and 42 use section dividers with a single headline, and slide 12 pairs two stacked bars to make a point about business travel.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2020
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and then frames the talk around S Curves, showing how technologies move from stupid to exciting to boring and asking what comes after smartphones. It moves into what happens when everyone is online, using ecommerce, TV and platform examples with simple bar and line charts, then covers the next S Curves, and closes with regulation and policy, including anti-trust, digital extraterritoriality and the idea that tech is becoming a regulated industry. The structure is a sequence of section dividers, one-idea slides with headline titles and short subtitles, and recurring diagrams such as the circles and S Curve. Slides worth studying include the S Curve sequence on slides 3 to 6, which builds one diagram across several steps, and the market share breakdowns on slides 79 to 81, where a stacked bar chart carries the argument. The deck ends with a thank-you slide that repeats the title details.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2018
decks.summary: Benedict Evans, an independent analyst and former a16z partner, gave a long talk on technology markets in November 2018. It opens with a title slide and an 'The end of the beginning' thesis, noting that most people are online while most of the money is not. The main sections follow in order. Market sizes examine ecommerce as a share of US retail spending, along with restaurants, gas stations, cars and advertising. New problems describe the internet moving from easy, low-capital categories to harder ones such as groceries, housing, transport, finance and health. Packets versus preference contrasts retail as logistics with retail as tastemaking. New layers cover machine learning and crypto as the next organising systems after search and social. The deck closes with a repeated 'The end of the beginning' section break, a 'What is this?' slide and a thank you slide.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2017
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a speaker card for Benedict Evans, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, presenting at the a16z Summit. It builds an argument in sections: first S curves, showing the PC installed base giving way to smartphones and the move from PC internet to mobile internet, then the scale and character of today's largest technology companies, then four emerging S curves to watch: AI, autonomy, mixed reality and cryptocurrency. Each section uses long runs of simple one-idea slides, with charts, diagrams and quotations rather than bullet lists. The talk closes on a return to the theme of innovation, a recap of the four emerging curves and a short thank-you slide. Slides worth seeing include the S curve charts that carry the first argument, the layered diagram of mobile and PC internet, and the single-quote slide that sets up the crypto comparison.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2016
decks.summary: This 78-slide talk by Benedict Evans, a partner-level analyst, presents his view of the mobile industry, with Andreessen Horowitz branding carried through its charts. It opens on a red title slide, then a bold orange statement, 'Mobile is eating the world.' The next section, 'Mobile deployment,' frames a shift from the creation phase of smartphones to a deployment phase focused on what can be built. The middle sections, 'A new kind of scale' and 'New kinds of computer,' compare the revenue and capex of Google, Apple, Facebook and Amazon with the old Wintel giants, and cover apps, imaging and frictionless computing. Later sections, 'Ecommerce' and 'Cars,' apply the same logic to retail and to electric and autonomous vehicles. The deck closes with a 'Thank you' slide. Each slide carries one idea, short headline-style titles, large simple charts and sourced footers. Section divider slides in a single accent colour pace the argument. Notable slides include the S-curve comparison, the Wintel versus GAFA revenue chart and the machine learning data-versus-rules slide.

decks.title: Benedict Evans conference talk, 2015
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a short framing before moving into its argument that mobile is driving technology's reach and scale. Early sections chart how smartphones bring more people online, using bar and line charts sourced from ITU, a16z and Ericsson, and then cover device costs and the growth of the mobile market. The middle sections argue that mobile has remade the tech industry, the internet and consumer electronics, with market share and unit-sales comparisons against PCs, cameras and games consoles. Later sections shift to how mobile dominates attention and how businesses are increasingly built around new technology, using Amazon and Wal-Mart as examples. The closing slides use Google Books frequency charts for railways, steel, computerization and software to argue that mature technology fades into the background, ending on the line that software is eating the world. Slides 4 to 7 and 14 to 21 are the most useful to study, as they show how a single chart is paired with one headline claim and a short source line.

decks.title: Nanigans recruiting deck, 2013
decks.summary: Nanigans created this internal culture guide to support hiring and fit decisions after growing from 35 to 100 people across four offices in just over a year. It opens with a Deloitte study quote on the value of workplace culture and argues that culture is a core pillar alongside industry, product and customers. A short narrative explains why the company had not discussed its culture before, followed by questions about what defines a great company and its employees. The team identified four themes: fast-paced, analytical, results-driven and collaborative. The middle sections pair staff photos, office life and social events with a repeated grid of descriptive words such as willing, invested and caring. Employee quotations from several departments follow, grouped under headings like Workhard, Playhard and Shared Experiences. The deck closes by restating culture as the basis for hiring, asking the reader whether culture matters to them, and ending with a recruiting call to action. Standout slides include the title slide, the one-line question slides that pace the story, and the photo-and-quote pairings in the middle sections.

decks.title: LinkedIn recruiting deck, 2015
decks.summary: The deck opens with a full-bleed photo of employees and the title 'Our Culture', then frames culture as who the company is and aspires to be, with a short introduction to five values: Transformation, Integrity, Collaboration, Humor and Results. It is organised as three kinds of transformation: of self (career growth, speaker series, wellness), of company (women in tech, employee resource groups, all hands) and of world (the economic graph, LinkedIn for Good, InDay). Each value then gets its own slide with a short definition, followed by the six operating principles and a run of employee portrait slides with one-line quotes. The closing section ties culture to growth, citing member milestones from 2 million in 2005 to 300 million in 2014, and ends with a call to join and a hashtag. Slides rely on full-bleed photography, short headline-style titles and brief captions, so the story is carried visually as much as by text. Slides 5 to 7 and 12 to 13 are useful to study for how section dividers and portrait slides are paced.

decks.title: Hootsuite recruiting deck
decks.summary: The deck is given to every new Hootsuite employee as a guide to the company's principles, history and culture. It opens with a title slide and short introduction, then moves through Core Principles covering vision, mission, culture, team and values. A Story section traces the founding from Invoke and the growth from 20 to over 600 employees. The Culture section explains the #BSU term and why people enjoy working there. The central Peepsbook is organised into three chapters, Who We Are, What We Do and How We Do It, with employee quotes, a list of suited traits, and short points on collaboration, trust and openness to failure. The deck closes with quotes from staff and leaders, including the founder, on curiosity and optimism. Its slides use large headline-style titles, one idea per slide, a consistent footer and simple charts. The Vision and Mission pages, with single large statements, and the flight path chart, which turns the growth story into one image, are worth studying.

decks.title: Buffer recruiting deck, 2015
decks.summary: The deck is a company culture document built as slides, titled The Buffer Culture and subtitled Powered by Happiness, version 0.6. It opens with a title slide and a note that the document is a continual work in progress, updated February 18, 2015. It then asks why culture matters, tells the origin of the values, and lists the ten Buffer values. The main body gives one slide per value, each with a short bulleted list of behaviours, covering positivity, transparency, self improvement, the no ego doer, listening, clarity, reflection, working smarter, gratitude and doing the right thing. Each value slide uses a headline style title and between four and five short bullets. The deck closes on the value of doing the right thing for customers and the company in the long term. Slides worth seeing include the value list on slide 5, which works as an index, and the listening slide 10, which shows how a bullet can be rewritten as a contrast of phrases.

decks.title: Zappos conference talk, 2009
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide for Tony Hsieh, Zappos CEO, presenting at Startup School on October 24, 2009, followed by a short personal background covering his early ventures and the sale of LinkExchange. It then moves to the company itself, showing a bar chart of gross sales from 2000 to 2008 under the heading about the power of repeat customers, and frames the business around three Cs: clothing, customer service and culture. The middle section develops culture and core values, including a list of committable values, and argues that vision and purpose inspire more than money. A later section draws on research into happiness, presenting three types of happiness (pleasure, passion and higher purpose) and linking them to business outcomes. The deck closes by repeating the question of what the company's higher purpose is, with the title Delivering Happiness and a contact slide. Slides worth studying include the sales chart, the three-Cs pyramid, and the three-types-of-happiness diagram, which uses simple graphics to carry the argument.

decks.title: Spotify conference talk, 2014
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a short greeting, then uses a road-trip metaphor: product vision is the steering wheel, and engineering culture is the engine. It defines culture as the shared values of an organization shown through members' actions, and cites Henrik Kniberg's view that culture is what people do without noticing. A diagram links values to culture and then to processes, artifacts, rituals and beliefs. The middle section walks through Spotify's own values, shown as four illustrated tiles with the value words listed beside them, and quotes Tim O'Reilly and Cory Ondrejka on why culture needs deliberate attention as a company grows. Later slides show how Spotify's agile processes and organizational model follow from its values, and stress regular self-surveys and fixing problems early. The deck closes with the line that culture leads and everything else follows. Slides worth studying include the road-trip image on slide 3, the values diagram on slide 9, and the Tim O'Reilly quote slide on slide 12, which pairs a portrait with a single large statement.

decks.title: HubSpot recruiting deck, 2013
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and then defines company culture as shared beliefs, values and practices, framing HubSpot's Culture Code as the operating system of the company. It then argues why culture matters for recruiting, contrasts how work has changed from past to present, and presents the seven points of the code in order: mission and metrics, solving for the customer, transparency, autonomy and ownership, people as the best perk, daring to be different, and recognising that life is short. Each principle gets its own section with short headline slides, quotes, and a few policy examples, and the deck is candid about gaps such as limited diversity and first-time managers. It closes with a recap of the seven principles, a line inviting feedback, and a thank-you slide pointing to the open discussion site. Slides worth studying include the opening definition slide, the then-and-now comparison table, and the one-idea-per-slide sequence on transparency. The deck is long, with many slides carrying a single line of text on a dark background.

decks.title: Netflix recruiting deck, 2009
decks.summary: This internal culture deck, later archived in favour of a newer version on the jobs site, opens with a title and a freedom-and-responsibility section divider, then states that the culture aims at excellence. Its core is a list of seven culture aspects: values, high performance, freedom and responsibility, context over control, highly aligned but loosely coupled teams, top-of-market pay, and promotion and development. Each aspect gets its own section, and the deck contrasts stated corporate values with the behaviours actually rewarded. Early slides use a framing device: a list of nice-sounding values followed by a slide showing the same values displayed at Enron, used to argue that rewards reveal real values. Nine named behaviours follow in a grid, with one slide per behaviour and short bullet points beneath. The deck then moves through talent density, the keeper test, freedom as companies grow, context versus control, compensation practices and career growth. It closes with a sequence of recurring section headers and a short line about continuing to improve the culture as the company grows.

decks.title: Apollo Global Management investor presentation, 2024
decks.summary: Apollo's 2024 Investor Day deck opens with a title slide, then a long forward-looking statements and disclosures page, followed by a welcome from the Global Head of Investor Relations and an agenda listing each presenter. The strategy section comes next, covering a decade of shareholder returns, progress against 2021 targets, the industry backdrop and new five-year growth targets. Business unit sections follow for asset management (investing and origination), credit, equity, real assets, capital formation, institutional capital, capital solutions, global wealth, retirement services, culture and financial strategy. The deck closes with a summary of takeaways and a Q&A session. It uses a consistent green-and-white template with a section divider before each speaker, large headline-style titles, and a mix of bar charts, timelines and simple diagrams. Several slides, such as the 2021 to 2024 targets scorecard and the Athene ecosystem growth bars, show how a single chart can carry a whole argument. Dense text appears mainly in the legal disclosures and some appendix-style slides. Slide 4 (agenda) and slide 9 (targets scorecard) are worth studying for how they handle information density.

decks.title: Sequoia Capital strategy presentation, 2008
decks.summary: The deck opens with a dark-humoured title, 'R.I.P. Good Times', and a 'Now What?' divider, then moves into a series of sections presented by different Sequoia partners. The first section, 'Wall Street: How Did We Get Here?', traces the housing-led recession, leverage, debt, and credit through charts of inflation, interest rates, household debt, home prices and derivatives. A second section, 'Main Street: Where Are We Now?', shows consumer spending, savings, debt service, falling advertising, retail, mobile and tech spending, with quotes from executives of EMC, Ingram Micro and SAP. A third section, 'Your Street: Where Do We Go From Here?', covers the venture financing environment, new fundraising and valuation realities, operating reviews and cost cuts, and a closing set of survival principles. The deck ends with 'Get Real or Go Home' and a Q&A slide. Slides are built around one chart or one idea each, with headline-style titles, while several sections lean on dense default-style charts and bulleted text.

decks.title: Mary Meeker, Bond conference talk, 2019
decks.summary: Internet Trends 2019 is a data-heavy talk by Mary Meeker of Bond, presented at Code 2019 on June 11. It opens with a title slide, a Bond branded cover, an agenda listing eleven sections, and a thanks slide crediting contributors, including Hillhouse Capital for the China section. A context section then frames the report around data, consumer and regulator concerns, and the roles of commerce, advertising and usage. The main body moves through users and smartphone shipments, then e-commerce and online advertising, followed by usage topics such as gaming, video, voice, images and on-demand services. Later sections cover non-US internet businesses, data-driven fulfillment and financial services. The deck relies on large single-metric charts with headline-style titles, each stating the takeaway with a directional word such as solid, slowing or accelerating. Slides with bar and line combinations and short quoted executive comments give the sections their rhythm. It closes with the China section and the remaining sections, and the final slides point to specific companies as examples.

decks.title: Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins conference talk, 2018
decks.summary: Mary Meeker's Internet Trends 2018 was presented at the Code 2018 conference on May 30, 2018, and published by the venture firm Kleiner Perkins. It opens with a title slide, a credits slide thanking contributors, and a context slide that frames the report around data, personalization, R&D spending, e-commerce, consumer spending, the consumerization of enterprise software, and China. A table of contents then lists twelve sections in order: users, usage, innovation and competition with scrutiny, e-commerce, advertising, consumer spending, work, data gathering and optimization, economic growth drivers, China, enterprise software, and USA Inc. and immigration. Each section opens with a short title slide, followed by charts that each carry one headline claim, such as the flat growth in smartphone shipments and the rise in internet users past half the world's population. The deck is built around data slides with headline-style titles and small-type source notes. Slides worth studying include the smartphone shipment chart that pairs bars with a growth line, the section divider slides, and the contents slide, which uses numbered sections with page references.

decks.title: Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins conference talk, 2017
decks.summary: Mary Meeker's Internet Trends 2017 was presented at the Code Conference on May 31, 2017, and published by Kleiner Perkins. It opens with a title slide and a conference-branded cover, then a contents page listing eleven sections: global internet trends, online advertising and commerce, interactive games, media, the cloud, the China and India internet, healthcare, public and private internet companies, macro thoughts and closing thoughts. The early slides cover global user growth, smartphone shipments and installed base, and US time spent on digital media. Each section opens with a full-bleed divider slide followed by chart-led slides whose headlines state the takeaway in a short phrase with the key figure. Slides worth studying include the 'Global Internet Users = 3.4B @ 46% Penetration' chart slide, which pairs a bar chart with a growth line and a source footer, and the time-spent chart that shows mobile overtaking desktop. The deck runs to 356 pages, so this review covers only the portion of text shown and the first twelve slides.

decks.title: Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins conference talk, 2016
decks.summary: This is Mary Meeker's Internet Trends 2016 deck, presented at the Code Conference on June 1, 2016, and published by KPCB. It opens with a title slide, a conference title slide, and an eight-part outline covering global internet users, macro trends, advertising and commerce, video, image and messaging, voice and transportation, China, public and private company data, and data privacy. It then moves through these sections in order, using large statistic-led headline slides followed by sourced bar and line charts, with the growth figure in each title and a footer carrying the source. Acknowledgements to partners, Hillhouse Capital and others appear early, before the data begins. The sections on advertising, commerce and messaging rely heavily on contrasting slides that pair a generation or platform with its behaviour. Slides worth studying include the India user growth slide, which uses a single large italic statement with a line of supporting numbers, and the smartphone share slide, which places a stacked chart beside a dual-axis chart. The deck is long, and the text provided runs only to slide 107.

decks.title: Mary Meeker, Kleiner Perkins conference talk, 2015
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide, a conference-specific cover and an outline that lists eight sections: internet adoption, key internet trends, re-imagining enterprise and consumer behaviour, America's evolving work environment, big internet markets in China and India, public and private company data, one more thing, and an appendix. It starts with user growth from 1995 to 2014, tracing internet and mobile penetration with simple pie charts and then comparing company market capitalisations across two decades in a ranked table. The middle sections use a recurring structure of a headline-style title, a chart or table, and a short source line, and the enterprise section pairs a 'then' and 'now' panel for each software category. Later sections cover messaging platforms, user-generated content, drones, cyber security, labour market statistics and the growth of on-demand work. The deck is long, and most of its slides are dense data pages rather than visual statements. Slides worth studying include the outline, the market capitalisation comparison, and the then-and-now enterprise panels.

decks.title: Bond report-style deck, 2025
decks.summary: This 340-page trends report from BOND, the investment firm co-authored by Mary Meeker, opens with a title slide, a date and author page, and a Context page explaining how the data set grew from a few charts. It then presents an outline of seven themes: a framing section on why change feels faster than ever, followed by user, usage and capital expenditure growth, AI model compute and inference costs, usage and loss growth, monetization threats from competition and China, physical world ramps, global internet user growth, and changes to work. Before those themes, the deck offers an overview of technology and geopolitics, a long history of compounding technology and knowledge distribution, and a timeline of AI milestones from 1950 onward. It is built almost entirely from charts, each with a headline title, subtitle and source line, and uses quotes from executives and researchers as section dividers. Later sections cover enterprise, government and research adoption before closing on benefits and risks.

decks.title: a16z crypto report-style deck, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide, a full-page disclosures slide, and a contents page listing nine sections. It moves through the crypto market's size and cycles, institutional adoption by banks, asset managers and payment firms, the growth of stablecoins, applications such as decentralized exchanges, real-world assets and prediction markets, blockchain infrastructure and throughput, the convergence of crypto with AI, the US regulatory environment, and a preview of a live dashboard. Each section opens with a numbered divider slide, and most content slides pair a headline-style claim with a single chart or table. The closing sections give a list of nine forecasts for 2025 and beyond, followed by a call-to-action slide linking to the podcast, newsletter and social channels. Slides worth studying include the market cycle chart on slide 5, which annotates events directly on the data, the stablecoin payment comparison on slide 19, and the Bitcoin versus macro benchmarks chart on slide 8, where a highlighted correlation box carries the takeaway.

decks.title: a16z crypto report-style deck, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide, a legal disclosures page and a table of contents listing six sections. It then covers them in order: how big crypto is today, including active addresses, mobile wallet growth and an estimate of real users; why crypto has become a political issue, including bipartisan quotes, swing-state search interest, regulation and central bank digital currencies; the maturity of infrastructure, including multichain flows, cheaper Ethereum layer-two fees, account abstraction and zero knowledge proofs; the key applications emerging, including stablecoins, AI, NFTs, DeFi, prediction markets, DePIN, gaming and social; what is known about builders; and finally a look at what comes next. Each section opens with a full-bleed divider slide carrying a numbered label. Most content slides use a headline-style title stating the takeaway, followed by one large chart or a few data callouts with source notes beneath. The deck closes with forward-looking thoughts, a price-cycle chart and a resources page.

decks.title: a16z crypto report-style deck, 2022
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and frames web3 as the third era of the internet, contrasting it with the open protocols of the first era and the siloed platforms of the second. It then explains why web3 matters, covering the flaws of today's internet, the extractive behaviour of web2 companies, property rights, and value alignment across network participants. A section on cycles of innovation follows, showing how price, interest, new ideas and startups feed one another. The main body surveys layer 1 blockchains, layer 2 scaling, DeFi, stablecoins, NFTs, web3 gaming and DAOs, each with its own divider slide and a run of data charts. The closing section lists real-world projects and predictions for the coming year, and the deck ends with a long disclosure page. Notable slides include the opening frame defining web3 in three numbered columns, the value-share slide that pairs one line of type with a simple graphic, and the cycles slide with three stacked charts and one short headline.

decks.title: Anthropic pitch deck, 2023
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide naming Anthropic, PBC and co-founder and President Daniela Amodei, then an introduction that describes the company as an AI safety and research company, a Public Benefit Corporation based in San Francisco. It states a mission of building reliable, steerable and interpretable AI systems. The middle section shows the company's research credentials, including its founders' work on GPT-3, a 'Helpful, Honest, and Harmless' framework, more than fifteen safety papers and a selection of research titles, followed by press and expert reactions to its Claude assistant. It then covers product traction through private beta customers, inbound interest and a waitlist, listing possible use cases, and a fundraising slide showing Series A, Series B and planned Series C funding by year. The closing slides argue that demand exceeds capacity, show the office and headcount, and end with a hiring slide listing engineering, security, business and product roles. Slides worth studying include the mission slide, which reduces the message to three stacked terms, the fundraising timeline, and the funnel-style diagram on the demand slide.

decks.title: WeWork investor presentation, 2021
decks.summary: The deck opens with a long disclaimer covering forward-looking statements, non-GAAP measures and the proposed business combination with BowX Acquisition Corp, then moves to the Q2 2021 results title slide. The main body runs in order: WeWork's network footprint of locations, members and desks; market context comparing flexible office adoption to e-commerce in retail; Q2 sales performance and the All Access product; a partnership with Cushman & Wakefield; the business transformation over the past 18 months; Q2 revenue and financial results; pro forma liquidity; management projections for memberships, occupancy, revenue and Adjusted EBITDA; market share by city; and finally methodology, non-GAAP definitions and additional information. Slides that repay study include the network overview, the market context slide that frames the argument with a clear analogy, the 18-month transformation comparison and the pro forma liquidity bridge. The closing is mostly legal and reference material rather than a call to action.

decks.title: WeWork investor presentation, 2021
decks.summary: The deck opens with a legal disclaimer and forward-looking statements covering the proposed business combination between WeWork and BowX Acquisition Corp., followed by presenter introductions and a contents page. It then moves into a section on WeWork and the future of work, covering the leadership team, company values, global network and scale, the platform and its growth drivers, the path to recovery after 2020 cost cuts, membership mix and enterprise customers, and offerings such as All Access, Marketplace and Platform. A financial and transaction section follows, with revenue and Adj. EBITDA projections through 2024, revenue by geography and product, unit economics for mature locations, liquidity and cash flow, the capital structure, transaction terms, pro forma valuation, sources and uses, and board composition. An appendix defines the key terms and metrics. The deck closes on its financial and transaction summary and definitions. Several slides pair a single headline claim with a chart or table, which makes the logic easy to follow.

decks.title: WeWork investor presentation, 2020
decks.summary: The deck is a short March 2020 update from WeWork's parent, The We Company, prepared during the early COVID-19 period. It opens with a title slide and then a forward-looking statement that withdraws earlier 2020 targets. A disclaimer slide follows, covering forward-looking statements, third-party data and non-GAAP measures. The main content sections are the leadership team, a three-stage strategy (short, mid and long term) and the five-year targets for 2024. The closing slide shows pro forma cash and cash commitments as a waterfall chart, tied to SoftBank financing that is subject to conditions. The strongest slides to study are the targets slide, which pairs four large headline metrics with footnoted definitions, and the liquidity waterfall, which shows how each source of cash adds or subtracts from the total.

decks.title: Dwolla pitch deck, 2013
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a one-line solution statement: Dwolla lets anything connected to the internet move money quickly, safely and cheaply. It then shows growth through a list of use cases, from individuals and schools to banks and developers, before introducing the founders and the origin of the company in the credit card fee problem. The middle sections build the case in order. A diagram shows how card payments flow and where fees accumulate. A list of problems with existing payment rails is grouped under cost, speed, fraud and bank dependence. A diagram of the Dwolla flow includes a real-time settlement step. Later slides cover the end-to-end product, the technology, the network's advantages, and the market opportunity in the US and globally. The deck closes with a 2013 hiring and expansion plan, a references slide and a closing title.

decks.title: YouTube pitch deck
decks.summary: The deck opens on a title slide with the tagline 'Broadcast Yourself' and a purpose statement: to become the primary outlet for user-generated video, letting anyone upload, share and browse it.
