It then names the problem: video files are too large to e-mail or host, lack a common format, and exist as isolated files. The solution slide describes uploading to a service that serves content to viewers, converts videos to Flash Video, and links users, videos and communities together. The market slide cites cheaper digital video recording and home broadband reaching critical mass. A competition slide names existing video sites. Product development and sales and distribution slides list planned features and revenue routes, including advertising, premium member features and paid content. The team slide profiles the three founders and their backgrounds. The deck closes with a metrics slide noting a June 11th launch and a claim of leading the space. Its slides are short and built around headline-style statements, and the market and solution slides are the most useful to study for structure.

decks.title: Crew (as ooomf) pitch deck
decks.summary: The deck opens with the title slide and the line "Average is over," then introduces ooomf as a premium marketplace of mobile and web talent where the talent picks the work. It moves to traction, showing a monthly project-value chart from February to August 2013 with 30% month-to-month growth. Next it argues for quality, comparing a $5,000 average project budget with an industry average of $500. The core product is explained in three numbered steps: pitching inspiration, automatic budget recommendation, and the single best pro coming to you, supported by points on no bidding, no spam and no price wars. Market sizing follows, with online contractor billings rising from $1B in 2012 to $4B in 2014, then the vision statement and a team slide listing founders' backgrounds. Investors and advisors are named, a designer's testimonial and earnings figure appear across two slides, and the deck ends with a $100MM project booking target for 2015 and a repeat of the title slide. Slides on traction, the three-step product flow and the market chart are the clearest examples of the format.

decks.title: Square pitch deck, 2011
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and then a one-page proposition covering market size, management, pricing, business model and defensibility. It then runs through the management team, the mobile payments market, the product and its technology, the value offered to users versus traditional and online card processing, and customer acquisition plans. Competition and defensibility come next, followed by a financial model with projections and an investment case with proposed funding rounds. It closes with exit strategies, covering M&A prospects and a potential IPO. An appendix holds financial assumptions, comparable company margins, valuation multiples, responses to investor concerns, partnerships, vision and market analysis. Slides worth studying include the market slide, which pairs a growth chart with opportunity, market change and positioning columns, the value comparison table on slide 6, and the financial scenarios on slide 9. The deck relies on tables, charts and short headline-style titles, and most slides carry one argument.

decks.title: Shopify investor presentation, 2016
decks.summary: The deck opens with headline metrics of more than 200,000 active merchants and over $1.9 billion in gross merchandise volume in Q3 2015. A safe harbour statement on forward-looking claims and non-GAAP measures follows. It then covers the company's multi-channel commerce platform and its market of entrepreneurs, small and mid-sized businesses, and larger brands. A market-sizing slide sets a global total addressable market against current core geographies. Next comes a company history in the form of a Build-a-Business timeline, along with the partner ecosystem of app developers, theme designers, and agencies. The financial section shows revenue, monthly recurring revenue, and GMV growth with year-on-year comparisons, a gross profit slide, and an operating leverage slide tracking expenses as a share of revenue. Growth vectors and investment highlights come next, and the deck closes with the line 'Make commerce better for everyone.' An appendix reconciles non-GAAP figures to GAAP.

decks.title: Intercom pitch deck
decks.summary: The deck opens with a DRAFT title slide, then introduces the founding team and their track record in software design, writing and prior product launches. It moves to the problem: building meaningful relationships with customers is hard for SaaS providers, and existing tools for research, messaging and email fall short. The solution slide describes Intercom as a simple install that offers customer browsing, individual customer research, in-app messaging and relationship tracking. Market sizing follows, then a landscape slide groups competitors by category, such as social media management, customer feedback, email campaigns and user analytics. The progress slide reports a product in development and testing, a public beta plan and early beta feedback. The closing ask seeks a $600k convertible note, the 18 months of runway it buys and the plan for a further round. The final slide is an advertisement for a third-party funding deck collection and the agency that made the deck.

decks.title: Facebook (as thefacebook) sales deck, 2004
decks.summary: The deck opens with a cover and a quoted press clipping from The Stanford Daily describing how the site has swept through campus. It then explains what thefacebook.com is, an online directory linking students, alumni, faculty and staff at colleges. Next it covers the user profile, the intra-school and inter-school networking features, and the school launch timeline in two tables, one for Ivy League schools and one for others. The audience section sizes the college market and its spending, followed by a series of user demographics and site usage slides with figures from March 2004. A user growth slide describes the trend in plain terms. The sales part follows, covering online marketing services, targeted advertising parameters, ad sizes and rates. It closes with a contact slide naming the company's CFO and a second press quote from The Harvard Independent. Slides worth studying include the demographic breakdown slides, which use one large figure per slide, and the school launch tables, which present a timeline as a simple grid.

decks.title: Contently pitch deck, 2013
decks.summary: The deck opens with a Series B financing title slide and then frames the market with a 2013 claim that content marketing is brands' top digital priority, followed by a survey chart showing creating original content as the leading challenge for marketers. A quote from Forbes positions Contently as platform infrastructure for brand publishing. The core product section shows a two-part offering: a network of more than 20,000 vetted freelance journalists and a cloud-based content creation software suite, illustrated with a journalist profile and a workflow screen. The middle sections cover company metrics in a revenue chart, customer pipeline value, and a strategy slide describing the aim to own the full value chain from talent to creation to distribution. A roadmap slide lays out the Series A and Series B timeline and planned expansion areas. The deck closes with a snapshot of founders, investors, key employees, advisors, technology stack and capital raised to date, ending on a short tagline slide. Several figures and plans are redacted, which limits how much of the financial case can be read from the text.

decks.title: Coinbase pitch deck
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide introducing Coinbase as a hosted bitcoin wallet, then moves to a short overview of bitcoin as a new digital currency, highlighting instant, international transfers with no transaction fees. It then shows early market traction, with bitcoin transaction volume of about $2 million USD per day, and lists use cases such as peer-to-peer and international payments, micro-transactions, virtual goods, games, e-commerce and remittance. The problem is framed as current tools being too difficult to use, which sets up Coinbase as a simpler hosted wallet. A comparison slide likens Coinbase to iTunes for MP3s, positioning it as a consumer-friendly layer on a new format. Growth slides show daily signups increasing about 20% per day and roughly $65,000 USD in transactions during the first five weeks. The deck closes by describing Coinbase as a new payment network based on the digital currency bitcoin. The structure is short and sparse, with one idea per slide and simple headline-style titles.

decks.title: BuzzFeed pitch deck, 2008
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a 'Where We Are' snapshot listing traffic, a two-editor content model, a patent-pending core technology and monthly burn. It then sets out 'Where We're Headed', covering a one-stop shop for web buzz, traffic growth without hiring editors, a self-serve ad platform and the hires planned. The middle sections walk through the product: a 'Buzz Detected' sample feed, raw algorithmic buzz phrases, the user-generated and aggregated content streams, the web app, optimization metrics and a leaderboard. Next comes the revenue model, with separate slides on advertising as content, distributed promotion through widgets and ads, custom promotion on client landing pages and trend targeting. Competitors are placed on a media-versus-advertising map, followed by a 'How Big Can This Get?' vision slide and a team slide listing founders, advisors and staff with prior affiliations. The deck closes with a contact slide. Slides worth studying include the 'Where We Are' metrics slide, the revenue model overview and the competitor map, which places the company between media and advertising.

decks.title: Brex pitch deck, 2018
decks.summary: The deck opens with the Brex name and then turns to the team and investors, listing technology and finance leaders alongside backers such as Ribbit Capital, Y Combinator and several payments executives. It then sets the problem: entrepreneurs are often refused credit cards, and corporate cards offer little control. Market slides follow, sizing the card revenue opportunity across global B2B payments, the U.S. Fortune 500 and U.S. venture-backed companies, and explaining why technology companies are the initial focus. Product sections cover better data, better controls, receipt capture and ERP integrations, shown through annotated transaction screens. Later slides cover retention through rewards, referral-only private beta growth, a 'negative churn' customer graduation chart by funding stage, and a unit economics table with reference customers. The deck closes with a short investment value proposition and the Brex name again. Several slides pair a single chart or annotated product screenshot with a headline-style title, which keeps the argument moving from market to product to economics.

decks.title: Tinder pitch deck
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide for Match Box, a flirting game, then tells the story of Matt, who sees someone he likes at a party but does not approach her because he fears rejection. It presents the product as the solution: users like people nearby and get connected when the feeling is mutual, with sign-in through Facebook. The middle slides walk through the core experience in sequence: a Like or Not card screen showing shared interests and friends, a matches list showing who likes you back, and a chat screen where two matched users begin talking. The next slide covers the matching signals, including hyper-location using WiFi rather than GPS, mutual liking, shared interests, and friends in common. The deck closes with a revenue slide listing in-app purchases such as two free matches, a fee to reveal each further match, paid virtual gifts, and paid placement higher in the Like or Not list. Slides 6 to 8 are the strongest for study, as they show the product flow with real screens and a short example conversation.

decks.title: Airbnb (as AirBed & Breakfast) pitch deck, 2008
decks.summary: The deck opens with a welcome slide carrying the company's contact details, then moves through a standard startup pitch sequence: problem, solution, market validation, market size, product, business model and adoption strategy. It then covers competition, competitive advantages and the team before closing with press quotes, user testimonials and a financial slide. The adoption strategy slide ties the offer to a specific event, Octoberfest, as a way to win early bookings in one city. The market validation slide sets two large figures side by side to suggest demand. The competition slide places the service against Craigslist, and the press and testimonial slides use short quoted lines in large type to carry the argument. Most slides keep a repeated header block with contact details, which makes the deck look more like a formatted document than a presentation. The financial slide closes the sequence, with figures shown on the page in the source text.

decks.title: Moz (as SEOmoz) pitch deck, 2011
decks.summary: The deck opens on a title slide naming Rand Fishkin as CEO and co-founder and setting the goal of becoming Seattle's next $1 billion company. It then gives a short company history and the funding raised to date, and explains how the company grew through inbound and organic marketing rather than paid acquisition. A market section follows, covering macroeconomic trends, the under-investment in organic marketing, and the analytics problems marketers face. Next, the deck defines the problems the product solves and the target customer segments. A metrics section reports 2011 revenue, subscribers, trial conversion, churn, margins and profit. The deck then describes the planned raise of $20 to $25 million, proposed board composition, business risks, use of funds, and a two-year team roadmap. It closes with potential acquisitions and a short case for why the company is positioned to win, ending with a call to join the company. Slides 3, 9 and 21 show how key numbers are presented as direct, scannable statements, and slide 13 turns a complex tool landscape into one clear argument.

decks.title: Mixpanel pitch deck, 2014
decks.summary: The deck opens with two problems: most people make decisions by guessing or by gut, and companies on mobile and web track vanity metrics such as page views and installs. It then presents Mixpanel as an analytics product for product and marketing teams, with a plan to expand into sales and finance and a mission to help the world learn from its data. The competitive advantage section points to a database engine built in 2010. Next comes a monthly recurring revenue chart over time with year-on-year growth rates, followed by a sales KPI slide and a marketing slide listing lead sources and spend. The expansion plan covers headcount growth, new leadership hires, and entry into New York and then international markets. A competition slide groups startups and incumbents by free and paid tiers. The deck closes with a financing history table listing seed rounds, a Y Combinator entry, and a Series A. Slides 7 and 8 are the most useful to study, since the chart and KPI layout show how numbers can carry a traction story rather than prose.

decks.title: Mint pitch deck, 2007
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide naming the four founders and a date in April 2007, followed by a product overview of the Mint personal finance application covering transactions, goals and net worth tracking. It then introduces the team and advisors, sizes the US market and its addressable opportunity, and compares Mint with its key competitor Wesabe and with potential entrants. Further sections cover value to users and to partner companies, user acquisition phases, the business model based on referral fees and future advertising, and a financials section with projected revenue, expenses and earnings. Later slides set out the exit strategy, risks and mitigations, competitive response and the financial assumptions behind the model, with a multiples analysis used to estimate exit value. The deck closes with a Q&A agenda and a risks table. Slides worth studying include the market size funnel on slide 4, the partner comparison table on slide 7, and the risks and mitigation grid on slide 13, which pair each risk with a concrete response in a single view.

decks.title: foursquare pitch deck, 2009
decks.summary: The deck opens by defining foursquare as a mix of friend-finder, social city guide and social game, then explains that it runs on website, iPhone app, SMS and API. It moves through the core product in order: friend finding, check-ins as the basic action, points and mayorships, a leaderboard, tips as short recommendations, and badges tied to time and place. Real examples of local merchants rewarding their mayors appear as proof that venues already use the mechanic. The middle section turns to business, setting lead generation as the primary revenue model and listing secondary streams such as sponsored badges, redeemable points and banner placements. It closes with a sample user profile showing 30-day stats and a trivia slide covering city coverage, platforms, the API beta and the two-person team. Slides 6, 11 and 12 are the most worth studying: slide 6 shows how customer quotes can carry a product story, slide 11 frames revenue around a measurable offer metric, and slide 12 gives concrete examples for each revenue idea.

decks.title: Front pitch deck, 2016
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a problem statement: business communication still runs on email built for personal use, with a stated 215 billion business emails sent per day. It then presents the solution, a collaborative multichannel email client for teams, followed by a competitive landscape slide placing messaging experience against business readiness. Next come a use case showing shared inboxes as the entry point, a slide of selected customers with quoted feedback, and traction slides covering monthly recurring revenue growth, churn, and a land-and-expand retention chart. The team and capital efficiency sections describe the founders, their backgrounds, and spending to date. The deck then covers acquisition channels, a product roadmap, financial projections for 2016 and 2017, the Series Seed and Series A funding history, and the opportunity in internal communications. It closes with a single thanks slide. Slides worth studying include the traction charts on slides 8 and 9, the shared inbox volume chart on slide 5, and the roadmap grid on slide 17.

decks.title: Mattermark pitch deck, 2014
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title and a one-line mission to organize the world's business information, then frames the problem: professionals lack a reliable way to ask business questions and get data-backed answers. It moves through market context and a proposed B2B search product, then sizes the audience from venture capitalists and angel investors to sales and business development professionals and later consultants and bankers. Traction follows, with monthly recurring revenue growth charts, a 2015 revenue goal, and revenue broken down by use case. Later sections cover the core questions customers ask, the data needed to answer them, the number of companies tracked, and a pace target for coverage. The deck closes with the leadership team, with short bios for each founder and key hires, and a final title card. Several slides are worth studying for how they present growth as simple line charts with one headline number and how a single diagram maps data needs to user groups.

decks.title: Buffer pitch deck, 2012
decks.summary: The deck opens with two quotes framing social sharing as the most important trend in marketing, then asks how social can drive traffic. It moves to the product idea of queuing updates, followed by traction figures: paying users, annual revenue run rate, margins and user growth. A milestones slide lays out the timeline from web app launch through API launch and integrations to projected user and revenue targets. The business model slide covers freemium conversion, churn and customer acquisition economics, and the social media landscape slide gives market context on sharing volume and traffic. A slide on the effect of buffering cites a click increase, and later slides cover the plan to become a default sharing standard and a competition map sorted into categories. The deck closes with the team and advisors, then a contact slide. Slides worth studying are the traction slide, which uses short numeric bullets, the milestones timeline, and the competition slide, which groups rivals into labelled categories.

decks.title: OpenAI conference talk
decks.summary: The deck opens with OpenAI's mission statement, describing itself as a research and deployment company working to ensure artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. It then explains foundation model development, covering pre-training, post-training with techniques such as reinforcement learning from human feedback, and safety systems including usage policies, system cards and monitoring. Next it shows how people use foundation models through a dense slide listing use cases grouped into ideation, coding and data work. A section on the short term argues for gradual deployment so that people, policymakers and institutions can adapt over time. A slide on AI for science maps application areas such as climate modeling, fusion energy, materials design and advanced manufacturing, followed by a long-term note on AI accelerating science. The deck closes with a slide on safe and beneficial AI for science, energy and security, listing commitments to safety research, best practices, cross-industry collaboration and societal applications. Slides worth studying include the opening mission slide, the foundation model explainer, and the science application map, which uses a central theme with radiating sub-topics.

decks.title: The We Company (WeWork) investor presentation, 2019
decks.summary: The deck opens with a legal disclaimer and forward-looking statement warnings, then a company overview covering locations, desks, memberships and the flexible workspace model. It moves through its key principles and a strategy shift from founder-led growth to a centralized focus on core WeWork desk business with profitability, then reports operating metrics including occupancy, revenue backlog and net retention. Later sections explain the business model and unit economics, optimize the location fleet by maturity, enterprise mix and market, and show occupancy cohorts for non-mature and mature buildings. An appendix covers KPI definitions, glossary, occupancy trends and non-GAAP reconciliations. The deck closes with a supplementary diligence section that repeats the disclaimer and gives a cohort analysis of top seven markets. Slides showing the location contribution margin walkthrough and the occupancy distribution charts are worth studying for how numbers carry the argument.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck is NVIDIA's September 2026 non-deal roadshow presentation for investors. It opens with a title slide and a long safe-harbor disclaimer covering forward-looking statements and non-GAAP measures, then moves into the company overview, describing NVIDIA as a full-stack AI factory platform and setting out its unique position across workload breadth, co-design, the CUDA ecosystem, deployment and global reach. A recent-events slide lists announcements since the last earnings report, followed by sections on capital returns and strategic investments, the full-stack platform, ecosystem customers, financial capacity and commitments, token economics, and product segments including Vera CPU, Groq 3 LPX, networking, NVLink Fusion and CUDA. Later sections cover residual value of GPUs, open models, Nemotron, physical AI and a closing summary of compounding growth. Slides worth studying include the per-gigawatt revenue chart on slide 11, the token economics comparison on slide 10, the networking growth chart on slide 17 and the GPU residual value curve on slide 22, all of which use charts to carry the argument.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide for the June 24, 2026 Annual Stockholder Meeting, followed by a long cautionary statement on forward-looking statements and product availability. It then sets out the agenda: procedural items, proposals and voting, a business update from founder and CEO Jensen Huang, preliminary voting results and a question-and-answer session. The proposals section runs across several slides, listing three management proposals (director elections, executive compensation and auditor ratification) and four stockholder proposals with their lead proponents. The business update summarises fiscal 2026 results in a compact table of revenue, gross margin, operating income and diluted EPS, each set against the prior year. A chart slide compares inference performance and token cost across GPU systems, using a dual-axis plot that makes a cost argument visually. A short section introduces the Vera Rubin platform and early adopters, and the deck closes with the voting result and Q and A. Slides 15 and 16 carry no extracted text, so they are likely image-led.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a long forward-looking statements disclaimer, then sets out NVIDIA's shift from chips to an AI infrastructure company. The middle sections cover the market case, citing $3-4 trillion of AI infrastructure spend by 2030 and growth drivers across cloud, enterprise and physical AI, then show the CUDA-X platform stack and token-usage growth. Further sections cover physical AI computing (training, simulation and deployment across robotics, autonomous vehicles and factories), an annual product roadmap from Blackwell through Rubin to Feynman, MLPerf benchmark wins, and a partnership with OpenAI for at least 10 gigawatts of infrastructure. The deck closes on that OpenAI partnership slide, which sets out the investment terms and spend per gigawatt. Slides 4, 10 and 12 are worth studying for how they use dense but structured data, a roadmap grid and benchmark charts to carry the argument.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2025
decks.summary: The deck is the slide set for NVIDIA's 2025 Annual Stockholder Meeting, held June 25, 2025. It opens with a title slide and a forward-looking statements disclaimer, then moves to a welcome and an agenda. The middle section covers management proposals on director elections, executive compensation, auditor ratification and a charter amendment, followed by three stockholder proposals with their lead proponents named. A business update follows, led by a short section that frames NVIDIA's shift from GPU chips to AI infrastructure. It includes a table comparing FY24 and FY25 results on revenue, gross margin, operating income and diluted EPS, plus product-line slides for Blackwell systems and an architecture overview. The deck closes with preliminary voting results, adjournment and a Q&A slide. Slides worth studying include the FY25 results table, which keeps four metrics in a clean comparison, and the architecture slide, which groups a wide product range under one heading.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a forward-looking statements disclaimer and a non-GAAP notice, then a company overview stating NVIDIA's installed base and developer reach. It moves through the GPU's history, the shift to accelerated computing, and the idea of AI factories as a new class of data center. Core sections cover the full-stack platform, networking for scale-up and scale-out, CUDA libraries with speedup figures, energy efficiency per token, and scaling laws for training and inference. A roadmap slide sets out a one-year product cadence, followed by market reach across industries, enterprise and industrial AI adoption, and sovereign AI partners. The financial section shows revenue, operating income and margin, cash flow, capital allocation, and a market platform breakdown, with reconciliation tables in the appendix. The closing slides are reconciliation tables. Slides 5, 6 and 14 are good examples of headline-led framing, and slides 9, 16 and 26 show how charts carry the argument.

decks.title: NVIDIA keynote, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a forward-looking statements disclaimer, then moves into the keynote proper. It presents NVIDIA's CUDA libraries and their expansion into new markets, followed by generative AI use cases such as digital humans, customer service agents and regional language models. Product announcements come next, including new RTX AI PCs, the Blackwell GPU architecture, and a sequence of charts tracking AI compute gains, energy reduction per model training and per token generated over eight years. Networking is covered through NVLink switches and Spectrum-X Ethernet, with a roadmap slide running from Hopper through Blackwell, Blackwell Ultra and Rubin, each laid out as a platform of GPU, CPU, NVLink, NIC and switch. Robotics and simulation tools, including Isaac, Omniverse and GR00T, appear in the later sections. The deck closes with a sequence of product and partner logos and a final section divider. Several slides are wordless or text-light, leaving the visuals to carry the message. The strongest slides to study are the energy-reduction charts and the one-architecture platform roadmap, where repeated structure makes the generational comparison easy to read.

decks.title: NVIDIA presentation, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a series of press quotes praising NVIDIA's GTC 2024 conference. It then moves into the core story: a 'new industrial revolution' framed around generative AI, a diagram of the NVIDIA platform spanning cloud, edge and developer ecosystems, and the announced Blackwell GPU platform with its performance and cost claims. Later sections cover NVLink interconnect, the NIM inference microservices software layer, and vertical applications in climate simulation with Earth-2, healthcare, robotics with Project GR00T, and Omniverse digital twins, with partner logos. The middle of the deck features analyst and press commentary and conference attendance figures. It closes with a CEO quote about the industrial revolution and a full forward-looking statements disclaimer. Slides worth studying include the platform diagram on slide 5, the single-idea Blackwell and NVLink slides, and the partner logo grid on slide 16.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2023
decks.summary: The deck opens with a forward-looking statements disclaimer and a short company overview covering NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform, its installed base and developer ecosystem. It then makes the case for accelerated computing as the answer to the end of Moore's law, moving through the waves of adoption (cloud, enterprise, autonomous machines, industrial digitalization), the generative AI opportunity, data center scale workloads and return on investment. Product and go-to-market sections follow, covering DGX Cloud, NVIDIA AI Enterprise, the Grace Hopper superchip and the one-year product rhythm. Financial sections then review revenue, gross and operating margins, cash flow and capital allocation by market platform (Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, Automotive), and the deck closes with a summary slide, a roughly one trillion dollar market opportunity, and appendix reconciliations of non-GAAP to GAAP figures. Slides worth studying include the platform overview on slide 4, the Moore's law chart on slide 5, the cost comparison on slide 13 and the margin chart on slide 22, where charts and single-claim headlines carry the argument.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2022
decks.summary: The deck opens with a forward-looking statements and non-GAAP disclaimer, then a company overview stating NVIDIA's accelerated computing approach and scale. It moves through the case for accelerated computing, including an Amdahl's law example and the end of Moore's law, then covers AI demand, the Omniverse metaverse platform, the full-stack platform and developer flywheel, and the new software and services. Financial sections follow, showing revenue, operating profit, gross margin and cash flow from FY2018 to 1H FY23, alongside a breakdown by market platform: Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization and Automotive. Each platform gets its own slide with growth drivers. The deck closes with a summary and a $1 trillion market opportunity framing, followed by appendix reconciliations of non-GAAP to GAAP measures. Slides worth studying include the Amdahl's law illustration, the market opportunity slide with its segment sizing, and the financial charts that pair bars with margin lines.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide for the Q2 FY27 investor presentation dated August 2026, followed by a dense safe-harbor section covering forward-looking statements, risk factors and the use of non-GAAP measures. The headline section comes next, with a revenue overview and a stream of single-metric slides on Data Center revenue split between Hyperscale and ACIE, gross margin, operating expenses, earnings per share, free cash flow and capital return. Each of these uses a simple before-and-after pair of bars or figures for Q2 FY26 against Q2 FY27, with a one-line headline stating the takeaway. A GAAP and a non-GAAP P&L table follow, then the Q3 FY27 outlook for revenue, gross margin and operating expenses. The back half is a series of reconciliation slides that bridge non-GAAP figures to GAAP, with footnotes explaining each adjustment, and it closes with a free cash flow reconciliation and a blank final slide. Slides 3, 4 and 8 are the strongest examples of the single-message layout to study.

decks.title: NVIDIA investor presentation, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a long forward-looking statements disclaimer covering risks and non-GAAP measures, a standard framing for an investor presentation. It then moves through a short agenda into an earnings summary for Q2 FY26, with highlights, a financial summary table and quarterly charts for Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, Automotive and cash flow. A Q3 FY26 outlook slide follows, setting out revenue, margin, operating expense, other income and tax guidance. A section on key announcements then covers partnerships and product news in Europe, healthcare, manufacturing, cloud, MLPerf results, open models, RTX PRO servers, robotics and Jetson Thor. The closing section reconciles non-GAAP figures to GAAP for the quarter, prior quarters and the outlook. Slides worth studying include the financial summary table pairing GAAP and non-GAAP columns with Y/Y and Q/Q changes, the one-number-per-chart quarterly bar series, the outlook slide with its explicit assumptions, and the reconciliation tables that tie each adjustment to a footnote.

decks.title: NVIDIA keynote, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a rhetorical question about European enterprise customers and a headline figure on ecosystem investment, then frames AI as a new industrial revolution. It moves through a layered view of Europe's AI economy, from energy and compute to models and applications, and then presents the Vera Rubin platform as a full-stack AI factory with reference architectures for modular data centres. A middle section covers agents, arguing that AI factories produce intelligence and agents put it to work, followed by open model contributions, customisation benchmarks for Nemotron models, the agent knowledge foundation, and CUDA-X tools. Later slides show industry examples across biology, manufacturing, design software, telecom, healthcare, robotaxis and robotics, and the deck closes with a consumer PC announcement supported by press quotes. Many slides are built as large single headlines over architecture diagrams, and benchmark slides use bar comparisons with a highlighted gain. The deck is dense with product names and logos, so it works best as a reference for how a keynote stacks platform, partners and proof points.

decks.title: NVIDIA keynote, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with the NVIDIA transformation from GPU chip maker to AI infrastructure provider and then moves through its main sections in order. These cover the CUDA-X library stack, 6G and AI-RAN signal processing, quantum-GPU computing, agentic AI and reasoning workloads, physical AI and robotics, and the Grace Blackwell NVL72 rack-scale systems. Partner data center projects from CoreWeave, Oracle, xAI and Stargate are shown with their power capacity and locations, followed by the Taiwan AI infrastructure announcement with Foxconn, TSMC and NVIDIA. Product sections cover NVLink Fusion for custom ASICs and CPUs, the DGX Station and RTX PRO Server, and the enterprise AI platform. Later slides focus on Isaac GR00T humanoid robot models and Omniverse digital twins, including a Kaohsiung City twin. The deck closes with a single-line summary slide. Slides worth studying include the CUDA-X library map on slide 5, the rack-scale hardware reveal on slide 14, and the partner data center slides on 16 to 19, where each site is labelled with its power figure in one consistent layout.

decks.title: NVIDIA keynote, 2025
decks.summary: The deck is a keynote given at GTC Paris 2025 and opens with a quantum-GPU computing slide before moving to Blackwell hardware. It then covers reasoning inference performance, the production ramp of Grace Blackwell systems, and a single architecture spanning cloud, enterprise, personal and edge AI. Mid-deck sections address European AI infrastructure, with telcos, cloud providers, supercomputing centres and a list of EU AI factories, followed by open models such as Nemotron, a developer platform called DGX Cloud Lepton, and industrial AI and digital twins for European automotive makers. Autonomous vehicles and robotics follow, with photo-led slides that show partners and products. The deck closes with a summary slide listing its main claims: a thinking machine, AI factories as new infrastructure, tenfold European infrastructure growth over two years, and agents and robots. Slides worth studying include the bar-chart slide comparing tokens per second per megawatt, the regional country-by-country stack diagrams, and the closing summary, which compresses the talk into a few short phrases.

decks.title: Anthropic course deck, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a short history of Anthropic, marking founding, model releases and research milestones on a timeline. It then sets an agenda covering why measurement matters, the company's approach to AI development and the themes of agents, safety and evaluation. The middle section covers the Responsible Scaling Policy: what it is, its goals, the AI Safety Levels and the stated preparation for ASL-3. A section on measuring capabilities follows, showing benchmark saturation, task completion time relative to humans, and comparisons of Claude 3.5 Sonnet with OpenAI o1 on SWE-bench Verified and Aider benchmarks, with cost per token noted. A case study on computer use includes demo videos, then practical safety measures and lessons from the first year. The deck closes with future directions in scaling governance, capability measurement and academic collaboration, followed by a question slide and a thank-you slide. Several slides use section dividers and agenda lists to orient the audience, and benchmark slides pair a headline claim with a short definition of each test.

decks.title: NVIDIA keynote, 2025
decks.summary: The deck is the keynote presentation from NVIDIA GTC 2025. It opens with headline growth figures for Hopper and Blackwell GPUs and data center revenue, then frames the industry around a computing inflection point. The middle sections cover the Blackwell system and inference performance, shown through a series of incremental benchmark charts that build from Hopper to Blackwell NVL72 with Dynamo. Further sections present the product roadmap through Blackwell Ultra, Vera Rubin and Rubin Ultra, followed by networking and co-packaged photonics, enterprise AI infrastructure and workstations, Llama Nemotron models, Omniverse and Cosmos for physical AI, and Isaac GR00T robotics. It closes with a summary slide restating the main announcements. Many slides use a single large figure or a stepped chart to carry the argument, and several roadmap slides compare generations side by side.

decks.title: Anthropic conference talk
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a short history of the speaker's shifting view on AI timelines, then lays out its main ideas: AI progress is driven mainly by scaling inputs, progress is predictable through scaling laws, and the largest systems are approaching human level. It moves next to a quick primer on contemporary machine learning, covering next-word prediction, the three-stage training pipeline of pretraining, preference modelling and reinforcement learning, and Constitutional AI. A section on why progress is easy and predictable follows, with scaling-law charts, representative compute and data scales, and comparisons to the human brain. It then reviews remaining challenges such as multimodality, reasoning, long-term planning and data limits, along with external objections. The closing sections explain why the speaker finds the trend concerning and why researchers entering the field can contribute. Slide-level visuals, such as the scaling charts and the compute usage plot, carry much of the argument, with short bullet text around them. The deck ends with a thank-you slide and a set of caveats on what the talk does not claim.

decks.title: Dropbox pitch deck, 2007
decks.summary: The deck opens with a single-line title slide, then frames the problem: in 2007, storing, syncing, sharing and backing up files remains painful. It reviews current workarounds, describes the ideal experience, and includes a short demo placeholder. Next it argues that the timing is right and that this approach beats existing options, comparing competitors such as Carbonite, Mozy, box.net and Foldershare across sync, backup, sharing, versioning and OS integration. A section on technical advantages follows, covering the Python stack, use of Amazon S3 and EC2, and a performance focus. The team slide introduces the two founders and their backgrounds. Later sections cover the business model for individuals and small businesses, a platform strategy for moving content from the desktop to web apps, and customer acquisition through early adopters, free accounts and viral sharing. The deck closes with a quoted endorsement from a startup ranking. The problem and workaround slides, which build the case in short bullet lists, and the competitor capability grid are worth studying.

decks.title: Uber (as UberCab) pitch deck, 2008
decks.summary: The deck opens by framing the state of San Francisco and New York taxi service in 2008, citing aging dispatch technology, fuel-inefficient vehicles and the medallion system as the problem. It then introduces UberCab as a members-only, one-click, on-demand car service with a geo-aware app and a luxury hybrid fleet. The middle sections cover key differentiators, operating principles, app and web features, use cases, user and environmental benefits, fleet and service area, technology, demand forecasting and market size. Later slides estimate the market, list target cities, set out best-case, realistic and worst-case outcomes, and sketch future optimizations and marketing ideas. The deck closes with a progress-to-date slide listing completed steps and the next milestones of buying cars, building the app and a February demo. Slides worth studying include the problem slide with its bold statistics, the market size slide with its single headline figure, and the progress slide that shows what has been done so far.

decks.title: NVIDIA presentation, 2026
decks.summary: This recap of NVIDIA's GTC 2026 event in San Jose opens with a title slide and a series of press and analyst quotes framing the event as a major moment for AI. The body then moves through the company's argument in order: AI as a five-layer system from energy to applications, the shift from training to inference, the economics of cost per token and tokens per watt, the Vera Rubin platform and Vera CPU, Dynamo and Groq for inference orchestration, agentic AI with OpenClaw and NemoClaw, open models and sovereign AI, the DSX framework for AI factories, and physical AI in robotics and autonomous driving. Several slides use large quoted headlines and short paragraphs to tie each section to a single idea. Event statistics such as keynote views and attendance appear mid-deck, and analyst and press reactions fill the later slides. The deck closes with a summary slide that restates the platform and the claim that agentic and physical AI are just beginning. Slides 7, 10, 12 and 13 are good examples of headline-driven structure with figures carrying the argument.

decks.title: NVIDIA keynote, 2021
decks.summary: The deck is the slide set for NVIDIA's GTC 2021 keynote by Jensen Huang. It opens with a list of the five themes of the talk: accelerated computing, the data center as the new unit of computing, AI as software that writes software, AI-on-5G, and autonomous systems. A slide of new technology names follows, then a platform overview with adoption figures such as CUDA downloads, developers and GPU apps. The middle sections cover scientific computing and the Omniverse collaboration platform, then data center architecture with BlueField DPUs, DGX systems and Grace CPUs. Later sections address AI software and frameworks including NGC, TAO, Jarvis, Merlin and Triton, followed by 5G and edge, security with Morpheus, and automotive with DRIVE, Orin and Atlan. It closes with a recap slide listing the new technologies, which the deck repeats at the end. Slides worth studying include the 'Data Center is the New Unit of Computing' build sequence (slides 17 to 21), which adds one layer per slide, and the BlueField GeForce NOW latency breakdown (slides 22 to 24).

decks.title: NVIDIA presentation, 2025
decks.summary: The deck is a recap of NVIDIA's announcements at CES 2025, built as a slide-by-slide highlights reel. It opens with a title slide and a run of press quotes from outlets such as Forbes, PCMag and CNET, which set the tone before any product detail. The main sections follow in order: consumer GeForce RTX 50 Series graphics and laptops, the evolution of AI from CUDA through generative AI to agentic AI, open-source AI agent blueprints, the Project DIGITS personal AI supercomputer with its GB10 specifications, Blackwell data center systems, scaling laws, and physical AI covering robotics, the Cosmos world model, and autonomous driving. Each product section pairs a headline claim with a short description and a spec or comparison graphic, such as the RTX 50 performance chart and the DIGITS spec breakdown. The deck closes on the physical AI theme and a summary of Blackwell production, with press quotes again at the end. Slides 4, 10 and 12 are the strongest examples of spec-led layouts, and slide 15 shows how a three-part system diagram can carry a whole argument.

decks.title: Anthropic conference talk, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide introducing the Anthropic Economic Index and its head of economics, then sets out a framing slide listing claims about AI as a general purpose technology with uncertain productivity and labour effects, followed by a slide pairing task-length capability growth with the need for better measurement. It then moves through its main sections in order: the privacy-preserving method used to analyse Claude transcripts, usage concentration across tasks, occupations, US states and countries, and a comparison of API and consumer usage patterns. A later section turns to growth and productivity, estimating task durations with and without AI and comparing the implied productivity gain with an OECD estimate. The deck closes with four summary points and a quotation about policy choices. Several slides are section dividers or carry only a single prompt-like line, so the deck relies heavily on charts and short headline claims. Slides 6, 14, 15, 16 and 22 are the most useful to study for how data is presented alongside a single takeaway.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a summary of Q4 and full-year 2024 highlights covering profitability, cash and operations, followed by a single-page-per-topic financial summary of revenue, margins, EBITDA and cash flow. It then moves through operational data on production, deliveries, storage and Supercharger growth, vehicle capacity by region, and core technology updates on FSD, AI compute and battery work. Other highlights cover Energy and Services, followed by a forward-looking outlook on volume, cash, profit and products. Photo and product pages on Cybertruck, the new Model Y, Semi, Megafactory Shanghai and the lithium refinery come next, then detailed key metrics charts and full financial statements, reconciliations and a closing page of definitions and forward-looking statement disclaimers. Several slides are worth studying: the highlights summary uses short bold-labelled blocks of text, the financial summary tables use a consistent layout across quarterly and annual views, and the vehicle capacity slide pairs a plain table with a regional market share chart.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a Highlights slide that lists profitability, cash and operations results for Q4 and full-year 2023 in short bullet points. It then moves through a Financial Summary and an Operational Summary, with quarterly and annual tables for revenue, margins, cash flow, deliveries, production and deployments. Next comes Vehicle Capacity, a table of installed capacity by factory, followed by Core Technology and Other Highlights, which cover FSD Beta, cost of goods sold per vehicle, energy storage and services. An Outlook slide sets expectations for 2024 volume, cash and product plans. A photo and chart section shows vehicles, factories and product lines. The closing sections hold key metrics charts, full financial statements with income statement, balance sheet and cash flow, reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP measures, and a legal page with webcast details, definitions and forward-looking statement risks. Slides 3, 6, 10 and 11 are worth studying for how each slide pairs a single headline message with a supporting chart or table.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2023
decks.summary: The deck opens with a summary of Q4 and full-year 2022 results, framed around record revenue, operating income and net income, followed by a note on the macroeconomic outlook and the cost reduction focus. It then moves through a financial summary with quarterly and annual tables, an operational summary covering production, deliveries, storage and charging, and vehicle capacity by factory. Core technology and other highlights cover Full Self-Driving Beta, vehicle software, energy storage and solar. The outlook section gives 2023 volume guidance and the long-term growth target, and the back half holds photos of factories and products, key metrics charts, and full financial statements with GAAP to non-GAAP reconciliations. It closes with webcast details, definitions and forward-looking statement disclaimers. Slides worth studying include the summary highlights page, the quarterly financial table, and the key metrics charts that pair trailing twelve month trends across several measures on one page.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2021
decks.summary: The deck opens with a letter-style highlights slide summarising 2021 deliveries, cash flow and profitability, followed by a table of contents. It then moves through a financial summary for Q4 and full-year 2021, an operational summary of production, deliveries and infrastructure, and a vehicle capacity overview by factory. Core technology and other highlights cover Autopilot and FSD, energy storage and solar, and services. The outlook section sets out growth and cash expectations. Photos of factories follow, then key metrics charts and the full financial statements, including reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP measures. The closing slides contain webcast details, defined terms and forward-looking statement disclaimers. Worth studying are the highlights and financial summary tables, the vehicle capacity table with its status column, and the trailing twelve month charts that smooth quarterly swings.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2020
decks.summary: The deck opens with a letter-style summary of 2020 highlights, covering volume, cash and profitability, followed by a short list of bullet highlights under those headings. It then moves through financial summaries for the quarter and full year, an operational summary of deliveries, production and deployments, and a vehicle capacity section covering the Fremont, Shanghai and Berlin factories. Core technology and other highlights follow, covering Autopilot, FSD, battery and powertrain, energy storage and solar. The outlook slide sets out the company's approach to volume, cash, profit and product for 2021. The back half is mostly reference material: photos of factories and vehicles, key metric charts, full financial statements, a reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP measures, and a closing section with forward-looking statements and definitions. Slides 4, 6 and 11 are the most useful to study for how a financial update pairs a summary table with a short narrative and a guidance section.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2016
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide announcing Tesla's plan to acquire SolarCity, followed by a long forward-looking statements disclaimer and a transaction overview covering pro forma ownership, expected close, approval process and per-share consideration. It then makes the strategic case in a sequence of headline-led slides: accelerating the transition to sustainable energy, creating an integrated sustainable energy company, solar installation cost trends, SolarCity's position as a solar industry leader, Tesla's record of innovation and vertical integration, product development priorities, and cross-selling through Tesla's retail network. Financial slides follow, quantifying $150 million of expected direct cost synergies in the first full year after closing and outlining capital discipline, cash flow and the combined financial profile. The deck closes with a process overview covering independent advisors, fairness opinions, disinterested shareholder approval and the board approval process, then repeats the title slide. Slides 4, 7 and 12 are the most instructive for how a single argument is carried by one headline and one chart or number.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2023
decks.summary: The deck opens with a forward-looking statements disclaimer, then moves to Tesla's mission of sustainable energy for all, framed by a comparison of the current fossil-fuel-heavy energy economy with a sustainable one. It then sets out a five-part plan to repower the grid, switch to electric vehicles, adopt heat pumps, electrify high-temperature heat and hydrogen, and fuel planes and boats, with investment and deployment figures for each step. Resource availability and mineral extraction follow. The middle sections cover vehicle design and manufacturing, powertrain, electronic architecture, software, full self-driving, charging, supply chain, factories, energy storage, impact and financials, with a capital allocation framework. The deck closes with a summary of the master plan goals, a Gigafactory Mexico slide and Q&A. Key slides include the 2050 sustainability investment stack, the Model 3 to next-generation vehicle manufacturing comparison, and the heat pump efficiency chart. Slides use large numbers and short headline-style titles, with charts that carry the argument.

decks.title: Tesla keynote, 2020
decks.summary: The deck opens with a September 22, 2020 title slide and a climate framing. A CO2 concentration chart leads to a note that the shift to sustainable energy needs more affordable EVs and energy storage, built faster and with less investment. It then sets goals: terawatt-hour scale battery production and more affordable cells. Bar charts of gigawatt-hour demand by vehicle segment and by heating and electricity category show the scale of growth required. The middle sections cover cell design, the cell factory, anode materials, cathode materials, and cell-vehicle integration, each with a cost-per-kWh reduction figure. Topics include larger cylindrical cells, a dry electrode process, silicon anodes, a diversified cathode approach, North American cathode and lithium supply, recycling, giga casting, and structural batteries. The deck closes with a 2030 target of 3 TWh, a stacked chart of cost benefits from vertical integration, an industry cost trend compared with Tesla's forecast, a call for suppliers to help, and a closing look at lower-cost vehicles and a high-performance model.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2024
decks.summary: The deck is the keynote from Tesla's 2024 annual shareholder meeting. It opens with a slide rebutting common market criticisms, then moves through sections on sustainability and manufacturing, battery durability, worker safety, total cost of ownership, vehicle production and product launches, charging infrastructure, energy storage and energy gross profit, services, and AI. Its central argument is that Tesla is more than a car company, with the AI compute and robotics slides leading toward its Robotaxi and Optimus efforts. It closes with a mission slide and a call to sign up for future events. Slides worth studying include the Model 3/Y battery retention chart (slide 5), which pairs a single data curve with a clear headline, the production comparison bar chart (slide 8), which ranks competitors visually, and the ecosystem diagram (slides 23 and 24), which builds the product map step by step with an added layer for the AI roadmap. Many slides use short headline-style titles and a large chart or image, with footnotes for sources.

decks.title: OpenAI course deck, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a welcome to the SME AI Accelerator in London on April 29, 2026, introducing three speakers from OpenAI and Enterprise Nation and Booking.com, followed by a short room-introduction exercise and a stated goal of leaving with one reusable solution. It then moves through an agenda covering ChatGPT foundations, responsible use and hallucination risks, and prompting, with a worked example of rewriting weak prompts into task, context and expectation. Next comes a demo of two workflows for a fictional London florist, customer feedback analysis and a spring promotion campaign, each with input, output and hands-on activities. After a coffee break, the session turns to building a custom GPT or project through a build recipe covering job definition, context, output format, guardrails and testing, followed by a showcase of local small business owners, individual build time, sharing and a closing call to continue learning. The slides rely heavily on step-by-step callouts, paired exercises and time-boxed activities, so the structure is easy to follow as a training run-through.

decks.title: OpenAI course deck
decks.summary: The deck is a workshop onboarding OpenAI's Codex coding agent for engineers. It opens with a title slide, a workshop overview covering goals, format and client choice, and an agenda of five lightning talks: introduction and setup, understanding agents, using Codex in the software lifecycle, delegating to agents, and how teams use Codex. The middle sections explain the agent loop and context window, compare IDE, app and CLI workflows, and map Codex to each stage from planning through deployment. A section on effective delegation introduces a four-field prompt template and AGENTS.md guidance files. Later slides show team integrations and customer quotes with metrics. It closes with three next steps, a hands-on exercise list and documentation links. Q&A slides separate each section, and many content slides use short bullet points with a few diagrams and tables.

decks.title: OpenAI course deck, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide for an SME AI Accelerator workshop held in Abilene, TX on April 17, 2026, followed by introductions of three OpenAI staff and a stated goal: to get comfortable with ChatGPT, see practical education workflows, and leave ready to build an assistant. It then covers an agenda, getting started with ChatGPT, responsible use, and which product tiers exist, before moving through academic, study and project planning, and career readiness workflows. A prompting fundamentals section introduces a task, context, and expectation structure with a worked example and a pair activity. The middle section turns to building a reusable assistant, with a build recipe covering job definition, context, output format, guardrails and testing, followed by a hands-on build sprint, iteration clinic and share-out. The deck closes with feedback and community links, and an appendix describes ChatGPT Education and sample campus use cases. Slides worth studying include the task-context-expectation prompt framework and the five-step build recipe, which are presented as simple, reusable frameworks.

decks.title: SpaceX investor presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck is a roadshow presentation for SpaceX's proposed initial public offering, dated June 2026. It opens with a forward-looking statements disclaimer, then an offering summary covering issuer, size, price, use of proceeds and lock-up terms, followed by the company mission and an integrated platform overview across space, connectivity and AI. The main body runs through the space business (launch vehicles, reusability, cost per kilogram), the connectivity business (Starlink broadband and mobile), and the AI business (compute infrastructure, Grok, X), before covering the growth strategy, lunar ambitions and financial track record with segment revenue and capital expenditure. The closing section shows the revenue growth, margin and net income targets, and an appendix reconciles non-GAAP measures to GAAP. Slides worth studying include the market sizing bar chart on slide 13, the launch cost comparison on slide 24, the Starlink satellite and subscriber charts on slide 29, and the segment financials on slides 47 and 48. Many slides use large numerals and short headline claims, and a number of charts carry the argument directly.

decks.title: Vercel pitch deck, 2020
decks.summary: The deck opens with a tweet from a developer praising Vercel and Next.js, then frames a problem: frontend teams are slowed by disjointed development processes, difficult production infrastructure, and repeated regressions that stop teams reusing past work. It then presents Vercel as the solution, introduces Next.js with adoption figures, and describes the platform in three parts: production infrastructure, an intelligent edge network, and cross-functional collaboration. A slide on the Develop, Preview and Ship workflow walks through an example deploy preview reviewed by engineering, design and marketing teams. The closing section shows enterprise go-to-market traction and charts of paid product usage and Next.js adoption, with month-over-month growth figures. Several slides are short, one-line statements that carry the argument, and the charts are used to back the growth story.

decks.title: Postmates pitch deck, 2011
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide introducing Postmates as an on-demand local delivery service, followed by a team and company overview listing the founders, a $125K seed round, and early investors and advisors. It then moves to a live demo and a comparison table showing how Postmates weighs cost, tracking, time and effort against USPS, UPS, independent couriers, U-Haul and driving oneself. Market sizing comes next, with a chart of the roughly $72 billion US courier market and a note on its fragmentation, followed by a slide on adjacent markets Postmates could enter. Traction, a phased market discovery-to-lock plan, the business model and the technical architecture follow in sequence. The deck closes with a short summary of the opportunity, the San Francisco trial and the team, and repeats the title slide. Slides 5, 6 and 9 are the most useful to study for how comparison, market sizing and staged rollout are shown.

decks.title: Amplitude pitch deck
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a team slide introducing the CEO and CTO, both MIT-educated engineers with prior startup and big-tech experience. It then argues the problem: companies must measure user behaviour to improve products, and retention drives growth. Next it positions analytics as core infrastructure, using a Facebook retention study as an example of behavioural cohorting. The solution section describes Amplitude as a powerful analytics product for app teams, covering cohorting, raw data access and pricing at scale. Technical advantages follow, focusing on a claimed 20X data-volume advantage and deeper query capability. Market sizing uses Gartner and Redwood Capital figures on business intelligence and mobile analytics growth. A competitive landscape compares Amplitude with named analytics and mobile marketing tools. Traction, distribution through an enterprise sales process, and long-term advantages close the deck. Slides worth studying include the cohort-definition example on slide 6, the competitive landscape map on slide 14, and the single-claim tech advantage slide on slide 10.

decks.title: OpenAI sales deck, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and OpenAI's mission statement, then defines an AI Native University as one that integrates AI across campus life. It moves through a maturity model from individual use to AI-native university, then presents customer case studies: The Wharton School's campus-wide rollout, Arizona State University's usage figures and project list, and California State University's 500,000-user rollout. Faculty spotlights follow, covering a Harvard lecturer's teaching assistant bot, a computer science professor's research analysis work, a Wharton marketing professor's assessment method, and CS50's office hour data. A table lists popular GPTs in the California State University System. The middle section describes a six-step onboarding methodology, from leadership alignment through technical setup, use case labs, activation campaigns, usage tracking and recognition. The deck closes with three takeaways about AI in execution, curriculum and workforce, an invitation to the OpenAI Forum, and the presenter's contact slide.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a Summary page of highlights covering profitability, cash and operations, followed by a short letter-style narrative on the year. It then moves through financial and operational summaries, manufacturing and hardware capacity, supporting infrastructure, AI and software, services, other updates and an outlook. Photo and chart pages sit in the middle, followed by key metrics charts, detailed financial statements, reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP measures, and additional information with a webcast notice and forward-looking statement disclaimers. The deck is data-dense and table-heavy, with quarterly and annual comparisons side by side. Slides worth studying include the Summary highlights page, which pairs bolded headline figures with short labels, the Financial Summary tables with year-over-year columns, and the Outlook page, which organises forward commentary under short headings such as Volume, Cash and Profit. Several slides use a single large image or chart to carry the point. The closing sections keep reconciliations in a consistent layout so readers can trace each non-GAAP figure back to its GAAP source.

decks.title: Tesla investor presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a Summary and Highlights slide covering profitability, cash, and operations, followed by a Financial Summary and an Operational Summary with delivery, production, and storage figures. It then covers Manufacturing and Hardware, Supporting Infrastructure, and SI and Other Services, including FSD and Robotaxi metrics. An Outlook slide sets out priorities on volume, cash, profit, and product. A Photos and Charts section with product imagery and trend charts follows, then Key Metrics, Financial Statements (statement of operations, balance sheet, cash flows), and reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP measures. The closing Additional Information slide covers the webcast, defined terms, non-GAAP explanations, and forward-looking statements. Slides worth studying include the Financial Summary table, which compresses five quarters into one page, and the Key Metrics pages, where small multiples of quarterly and trailing twelve month trends sit side by side. The Outlook slide shows how four short headline-led themes can replace a longer narrative.

decks.title: Anthropic conference talk, 2023
decks.summary: The deck is a conference talk by Ben Mann, cofounder of Anthropic, titled Aligning AI with Human Values, with lessons from building Claude. It opens with a title slide and a mission statement: developing AI that is helpful, honest, and harmless. A short agenda follows, repeated as a recurring section marker that lists alignment, scalable oversight, and responsible deployment. The alignment section defines the three mission terms with brief sub-points and then introduces Constitutional AI as a sequence of defining principles, revising responses accordingly, and applying reinforcement learning. The scalable oversight section lists automated testing, expert red teaming, and crowdsourcing as methods. The deployment section covers strong demand at launch, data privacy, and a layered response to new attacks. The deck closes with a single line, Let's build safe AGI. Most slides are short bullet lists with headline-style titles, so the agenda slides serve as a navigational spine. Slides 4 and 5 repeat the same agenda text, and slide 12 is blank.

decks.title: SecurityScorecard recruiting deck, 2022
decks.summary: The deck is an internal culture guide, titled SecurityScorecard DNA, shared with all employees. It opens with a mission statement framing the guide as a shared playbook, then moves through a short overview of mission, vision, the purpose of culture, the customer, three strategic goals and the organization. Its middle sections cover the five [SCORE]card values (Solutions Focused, Customer Obsessed, One Scorecard, Resilient, Embody #SecurityDNA), each with anti-patterns and behaviors by seniority, followed by innovation and experimentation, and employee health, wellness and development. It closes with a call to apply through the careers page. Slides use short headline titles, one idea per slide, and sometimes a single quotation or image-led page. Slide 13 frames competition in a few stark lines, slide 21 sets out the three goals in parallel columns, slide 28 lays out a value with its anti-patterns and behaviors in a three-column grid, and slide 57 walks through a root-cause chain as a sequence of short answers.

decks.title: Netflix conference talk, 2018
decks.summary: This deck is a talk by engineer Brendan Gregg, delivered at the YOW! CTO Summit in 2018, about his more than four and a half years working at Netflix. It opens with a title slide and a brief framing, stating that the talk is a personal account rather than an official HR or PR guide. The middle sections cover his first meeting about a CentOS to Ubuntu migration, his job interview, the company's publicly documented culture, and Netflix values such as freedom and responsibility, context not control, and disagreeing openly. Each cultural principle is linked to a short personal experience, including the leap second bug, Java frame pointers, and crashing production. Later sections describe the cloud architecture as resilient and rapidly deployed, and warn about the brilliant jerk problem. The deck ends with takeaways and a thank-you slide. Its title-and-photo layouts for experience slides, which pair one bold claim with one image, and its large-type philosophy slides listing principles with minimal decoration are worth studying.

decks.title: Mitsui Chemicals strategy presentation, 2025
decks.summary: The deck opens with a cover and contents page that divide the talk between the group's portfolio transformation, led by the CEO, and a business strategy section for Basic & Green Materials, presented by a senior executive. It then outlines the aims of a planned split and the strategic position of a polyolefins integration with Sumitomo Chemical and Idemitsu Kosan, using a one-page map of plant closures, restructuring steps and partner collaborations. The middle section follows the business case in order: domestic polyolefin demand against capacity, the history of consolidation, the earnings trend of the existing joint venture, the ownership and business outline of the deal, integration synergies, green feedstock sourcing, and the profitability baseline. A business plan section links these to a 2030 operating income target and a cumulative cash flow bridge. The deck closes with a short vision statement and a standard forward-looking statements disclaimer. Several slides merit close study. The demand and capacity slide uses simple bar comparisons to show the excess-capacity argument at a glance.

decks.title: CD PROJEKT GROUP strategy presentation, 2022
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide for a strategy update on long-term product outlook, followed by a short company introduction covering who CD PROJEKT is, its core business in story-driven video games, its purpose, and sales figures of 65+ million and 20+ million copies. It then reviews transformation and growth since Q1 2021, including a new game engine, two North American acquisitions and board additions, and introduces a set of key directions and ESG ambitions. The middle sections explain the approach to talent and franchise expansion, then go through the project pipeline: Cyberpunk 2077 Phantom Liberty, Project Sirius, Project Polaris, Project Canis Majoris, Project Orion, a new North American studio and the new IP Project Hadar. A long-term product outlook slide consolidates these titles, followed by sections on multiplayer, TV and film, and a key takeaways slide setting out goals for three enduring franchises. The closing slide is a long legal disclaimer. Slides worth studying include the consolidated product outlook timeline and the key takeaways slide, which are simple, legible summaries of a complex pipeline.

decks.title: Prudential strategy presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and then a 'strong foundation' overview of Prudential's five businesses: Group Insurance, Individual Life, Retirement, PGIM and International. It moves to a scale view with headline figures on customers, assets under management and capital returned, followed by a description of the integrated model and its distinctive advantages. Strategy is presented next, anchored on four priorities covering focus on chosen businesses, capital optimization, global scale efficiency and geographic choices. Subsequent slides examine secular demand trends, retirement market leadership by country, PGIM's credit platform, and the Group Insurance and Individual Life businesses with market share and sales forecasts. The deck then covers portfolio rotation, the redesigned financial profile with cost targets, and the multi-year path. It closes with success outcomes and a long appendix of footnotes, forward-looking statements and non-GAAP reconciliations. Slides worth studying include the strategic priorities slide, which pairs four numbered pillars with short bullets, the market-share slide for retirement, and the Individual Life sales chart.

decks.title: Sonova strategy presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and a forward-looking statements disclaimer, then an agenda in four parts: introduction, strategy update, conclusion and Q&A. The introduction reviews the first six months under the new CEO, covering market and technology leadership, financial strength and recent product highlights, and sets out a demographic case for steady market growth. The strategy update covers the planned divestment of Consumer Hearing, a CHF 6 billion revenue ambition with five strategic priorities, the leadership team, R&D and innovation, an Asia playbook, channel strategy with wholesale and retail synergies, operations and productivity, finance and trading update, mid-term targets, and capital allocation. The conclusion restates the CHF 6 billion ambition for FY 2030/31 and the focus on hearing care. Slides worth studying include the market-growth slide with its population and adoption charts, the wholesale-retail synergy slide with its before-and-after proof of concept, and the productivity slide that ties four levers to a cost figure.

decks.title: Basic-Fit investor presentation, 2026
decks.summary: The deck is the Basic-Fit Capital Markets Day 2026 presentation, delivered by a sequence of executives: CEO René Moos opens with the company's history, growth record and a market overview, then the COO and CCO cover operations, franchising and member engagement, and the CFO closes with the financial framework. The middle sections describe the European fitness market by country, using penetration rates, competitor club counts and pricing tables. The operations section explains the cost model, staffless opening hours and break-even point, while the commercial section covers brand, creative testing, retention and member value. The financial section sets out the organic, inorganic and franchise growth levers, capital allocation rules, debt maturities and 2026 guidance, and the deck ends with a short thank-you slide. Slides worth studying include the consistent-growth KPI slide (slide 3), the market penetration slide (slide 8), the three-verticals growth slide (slide 34) and the 2026 guidance slide (slide 104).

decks.title: Lendlease strategy presentation, 2024
decks.summary: The deck opens with a title slide and an acknowledgement of country, then moves into a chairman's introduction and a statement of why the strategy update is needed: slow overseas construction earnings, long-dated overseas development projects, and the aim to recycle capital. Its core sections follow in order: a delivery section on simplifying the business and cutting costs, a focused structure with segment roles, an Australia growth section with pipeline and capability data, a financials section with historical pro-forma tables, a capital management section covering the capital release unit, allocation framework and buy-back, and a segment summaries appendix with supporting data. It closes with a summary slide, the analyst Q&A marker, and a disclaimer.
